Authors: most apparent variation is day-to-day fluctuation; assuming the mean treatment effect may be better than monitoring an individual's response. Bell, Irwig et al., Hypertension 2010. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20625081/ | source dated 2010-09 | OPENED | CITED
137	- D4-03-F56 | HOME BP trial rule and schedule (UK, n = 622, digital self-management) | Two morning readings for 7 days each month, entering each second reading online (TASMINH2 and TASMIN-SR method); after a minimum 7-day rehearsal period. Mean home BP fed back with a traffic-light system; "When mean home blood pressure was above target for two consecutive months", the prescriber was emailed to make the preplanned drug change. Home targets were clinic targets minus 5/5 mmHg (under 80 without diabetes <135/85; 80 and over <145/85). Result: clinic BP fell 151.7/86.4 to 138.4/80.2 (intervention) and 151.6/85.3 to 141.8/79.8 (usual care); difference -3.4 mmHg systolic (-6.1 to -0.8). McManus et al., BMJ 2021. https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7814507 | source dated 2021-01 | OPENED | CITED
138	- D4-03-F57 | Usual-care fall as a regression-to-the-mean signal | In HOME BP (F56) the usual-care group, recruited for clinic SBP >140, fell about 9.8 mmHg systolic (151.6 to 141.8) over one year without the intervention. Arithmetic: 151.6 - 141.8 = 9.8. The trial does not separate regression to the mean from usual-care changes; F26 and F27 show the size expected from regression alone. https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7814507 | source dated 2021-01 | OPENED | OUR ARITHMETIC
139	
140	### India practice context
141	
142	- D4-03-F58 | Home BP use and technique in North India (3 centres, n = 2,588 people with hypertension or caregivers) | 18.1% used home BP monitoring (20.5% urban, 8.5% rural). Only 24.7% of users recalled any training from a health worker; 75.2% learned from observation, videos or reading. Observed technique scored excellent in 15.9% of patients and 5.9% of caregivers; knowledge excellent in 0.4%. Mean scores: practice 62.3%, knowledge 40.1%. Batta, Mohan et al., Indian Heart J 2024. https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC11705592 | source dated 2024-11 | OPENED | CITED
143	- D4-03-F59 | 2026 ISH global guideline exists but home-schedule content not checked | 2026 ISH Global Hypertension Practice Guidelines published online 20 Oct 2026 (J Hypertens 44(12):2157-2188; Stergiou, Kario et al.). The PubMed record has no abstract; home BP schedule, thresholds and titration wording NOT OPENED. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42909506/ | source dated 2026-10-20 | OPENED | CITED
144	- D4-03-F60 | Japan guideline 2025 (JSH2025, the fund's home country) | Key updates per the guideline's highlights paper: universal BP target <130/80 mmHg, promotion of home BP monitoring, guidance on digital health. Home-measurement schedule details NOT OPENED. Ohya et al., Hypertens Res 2025 (full guideline Hypertens Res 2026;49:9-235). https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40877471/ | source dated 2025-08 | OPENED | CITED
145	
146	### Derived numbers for the loop
147	
148	- D4-03-F61 | Smallest real change between two monthly home means on stable treatment, derived from F11 | Within-person SD of monthly mean SBP 4.7 to 5.1 mmHg (TASMINH4, HOMEBP). SD of a difference between two months = 4.7 x 1.414 = 6.6 to 5.1 x 1.414 = 7.2 mmHg. 95% limit (x 1.96): 13.0 to 14.1 mmHg systolic. 80% limit (x 1.28): 8.5 to 9.2 mmHg. This is larger than the week-to-week figure in F34 (8.5 mmHg for two 7-day means) because month-to-month includes slow real drift and season as well as measurement noise. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40838357/ | source dated 2025-11 | OPENED | OUR ARITHMETIC
149	- D4-03-F62 | Single readings are nearly useless for a decision, derived from F10 | With a within-week SD of 11.8 mmHg for single systolic readings in treated patients, one reading has a 95% band of about +/- 23 mmHg (1.96 x 11.8) around the person's weekly mean, so a single reading of 150 is compatible with a weekly mean anywhere from about 127 to 173. Readings within one day are correlated, so averaging 28 readings does not shrink the error by the full square root of 28; use the empirical F33/F34 figures for means. https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12237135 | source dated 2025-08 | OPENED | OUR ARITHMETIC
150	
151	
152	## NOT FOUND / NOT SEARCHED
153	
154	- NOT FOUND: the 2026 ISH global guideline's home-monitoring schedule, thresholds and titration wording. PubMed has no abstract, and one web search found no summary (F59).
155	- NOT FOUND: an Indian study of seasonal change in home cuff readings. Only survey or visit readings were found (F31, F32).
156	- NOT FOUND: Indian data on within-person home BP variability (reading to reading, day to day). GRAND planned this analysis; only its control-phenotype and knowledge results were found (F40, F41).
157	- NOT FOUND: a formal statistical rule (control chart, CUSUM, Bayesian) used in a published home-BP titration trial. Trials used simple rules instead: mean above target for two consecutive months, 4 or more high readings in 2 weeks, or 3 of the last 10 readings at 135 or more (F13, F38, F56).
158	- NOT SEARCHED: the full texts of ESH 2023 and ACC/AHA 2017 for dipping and morning-surge definitions. The definitions here come from study papers (F46, F48, F50).
159	- NOT SEARCHED: the TASMINH2 full text for its exact self-titration rule (abstract only, F20).
160	- NOT SEARCHED: morning surge measured from home readings, and morning-surge data from India.
161	- NOT SEARCHED: guideline intervals between titration steps (covered by D4-02).
162	- NOT SEARCHED: reading-to-reading variation in South Asian home users.
163	
164	Direct fetches through Europe PMC, PubMed E-utilities and publisher pages are not counted; about 20 such query or abstract fetches were made.
165	
166	Searches used: 2

1	# D4-04 Why each safety check exists (agent: claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-14)
2	
3	## Digest
4	
5	The 12 facts that matter most:
6	
7	1. Creatinine rises on an ARB because blocking angiotensin II relaxes the efferent arteriole, so filtration pressure falls; the rise comes in the first 2 weeks and settles by 2 to 4 weeks (D4-04-F26, F27).
8	2. Accepted rise: under 30% creatinine (or 25% eGFR fall) continue and recheck; 30% or more look for dehydration or NSAIDs, then stop or reduce; no trial tested the cut-off (F21, F23, F27).
9	3. Rises below 30% still carry graded risk: death IRR 1.15 at 10-19%, 1.35 at 20-29% (UK, 122,363 people) (F22).
10	4. Recheck creatinine and potassium 1 to 2 weeks (NICE, UKKA) or 2 to 4 weeks (KDIGO) after starting or raising an ARB; the Indian IHCI sheets ask for no recheck (F23, F27, F34, F57).
11	5. Potassium: caution above 5.0 before starting; 5.5-5.9 recheck within 3 days; 6.0-6.4 within 1 day and stop the RAS blocker; 6.5 or more admit. Potassium sets the heart cell resting potential; the ECG can look normal (F24, F34, F35).
12	6. RAS blockers in the 2nd and 3rd trimester stop fetal urine, so the amniotic sac drains: lung hypoplasia, skull and limb deformities, death (F02, F54, F56). Stop within 2 working days; use labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa (F29, F30).
13	7. The first-trimester malformation signal (RR 2.71) shrinks to OR 1.14 against untreated hypertensive mothers (F31, F32).
14	8. Thiazide hyponatraemia: 2-year incidence 3.5-3.8%; HR about 4 in the first 30 days, 1.3 after a year; worse with age and low weight (F58, F61).
15	9. Chlorthalidone gives more hypokalaemia than HCTZ (6.0% vs 4.4%), no outcome gain; thiazide cardiac arrest risk rises with dose (F33, F37).
16	10. Amlodipine edema: 3.0% at 5 mg, 10.8% at 10 mg; arteriolar-only dilation raises capillary pressure; adding a RAS blocker cuts it 38% (F11, F65, F66).
17	11. Orthostatic hypotension affects about 22% of community elders (Kerala 9.6%), falls OR 1.73; hip fractures rise 43% in the 45 days after starting any antihypertensive; home self-testing works (kappa 0.90) (F39, F40, F42, F48, F50).
18	12. 180/110 without symptoms: 0-0.5% MACE at 7 days; emergency means organ damage; chronic hypertension shifts brain autoregulation upward, so crashing pressure is the danger (F68, F70, F72).
19	
20	Surprises: US labels give no numeric creatinine or potassium thresholds (F04, F06, F15); thiazide hyponatraemia is far commoner than labels say (F58); intensive targets do not raise orthostatic hypotension (F44), but the weeks after starting do (F48).
21	
22	## What this suggests for the product
23	
24	- Suggestion: schedule a creatinine and potassium test 1 to 2 weeks after telmisartan starts and after 40 to 80 mg, and block the next step-up until it is back (F23, F27, F34, F57).
25	- Suggestion: encode the creatinine rule as a trend (percent change from the pre-telmisartan value), not pass or fail: under 30% continue and recheck; 30% or more goes to the doctor with a dehydration and NSAID checklist (F21, F22, F23, F27).
26	- Suggestion: encode potassium bands with recheck windows (5.5-5.9 in 3 days, 6.0-6.4 in 1 day, 6.5 urgent), and ask about potassium-based "low sodium" salt and painkillers before telmisartan (F07, F28, F34).
27	- Suggestion: a pregnancy and contraception question every cycle for women of childbearing age on or about to start telmisartan or chlorthalidone; "pregnant" triggers a stop-within-2-working-days alert and a drafted switch for the doctor (F01, F29, F30, F57).
28	- Suggestion: for patients 60 and over, add a sit-then-stand reading pair (1 and 3 minutes) plus a dizziness and falls question in the 45 days after each step; a 20/10 drop flags the doctor (F38, F41, F48, F50).
29	- Suggestion: sodium test within the first month of chlorthalidone, prioritised for older, thin patients and the hot season (F58, F61, F62).
30	- Suggestion: ask about ankle swelling after the amlodipine 10 mg step and send it to the doctor as a reason to move to the telmisartan step rather than stop (F11, F65, F66).
31	- Suggestion: a reading of 180/110 or more triggers a rested repeat and a symptom checklist (chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, vision, weakness): symptoms go to same-day care; no symptoms go to urgent doctor review, never extra doses to bring it down fast (F68, F70, F71, F72).
32	
33	## Findings
34	
35	### Labels (US DailyMed): what each label says and why
36	
37	- D4-04-F01 | Telmisartan boxed warning: fetal toxicity | Boxed warning: "When pregnancy is detected, discontinue telmisartan as soon as possible." and "Drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus". Generic telmisartan label (Ascend/Alkem, made in India), revised March 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03, SPL 2026-11-04 | OPENED | CITED
38	- D4-04-F02 | Why RAS blockers harm the fetus (label mechanism and timing) | Label 5.1: RAS-acting drugs "during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy reduces fetal renal function and increases fetal and neonatal morbidity and death". Chain: less fetal urine, so oligohydramnios, so fetal lung hypoplasia and skeletal deformations; neonatal skull hypoplasia, anuria, hypotension, renal failure, death. Label 8.1: most first-trimester studies did not separate RAS drugs from other antihypertensives. If no alternative: serial ultrasound of the amniotic environment. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
39	- D4-04-F03 | Losartan carries the same fetal warning | Cozaar label 5.1 uses the same wording as telmisartan (2nd and 3rd trimester, oligohydramnios, lung hypoplasia, skull hypoplasia, anuria, death; discontinue as soon as possible). Year 2021 label text. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=9949448f-c3b9-44ee-94ed-c1aca8c90f39 | label revised 2021-06, SPL 2026-01-21 | OPENED | CITED
40	- D4-04-F04 | Telmisartan and the kidney (label) | Label 5.5: "As a consequence of inhibiting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, anticipate changes in renal function in susceptible individuals." Patients whose filtration depends on RAAS (severe heart failure, renal dysfunction) can get oliguria, progressive azotaemia, rarely acute renal failure or death. In ACE-inhibitor studies of unilateral or bilateral renal artery stenosis, creatinine or urea rose; "anticipate an effect similar" with telmisartan. The label gives no numeric creatinine threshold and no recheck interval. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
41	- D4-04-F05 | Telmisartan creatinine rise in trials is rare | Label 6.1: a creatinine rise of 0.5 mg/dL or more in 0.4% on telmisartan against 0.3% on placebo; one patient stopped for creatinine and urea rise. In 30 hypertensive patients with normal kidneys on telmisartan 80 mg (with or without HCTZ 12.5 mg) for 8 weeks: no clinically significant change in renal blood flow, GFR, filtration fraction or creatinine clearance. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
42	- D4-04-F06 | Telmisartan potassium (label) | Label 5.3: hyperkalaemia "may occur in patients on ARBs", especially advanced renal impairment, heart failure, dialysis, potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium-containing salt substitutes. Advice: "Consider periodic determinations of serum electrolytes". No numeric threshold. Mechanism: ARB blocks angiotensin II at the AT1 receptor, so less aldosterone drive, so less potassium excreted by the collecting duct. Telmisartan multiple-dose studies: "no clinically significant changes" in serum potassium, sodium, glucose or uric acid. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
43	- D4-04-F07 | Low-salt substitutes are a potassium source | Telmisartan label names "potassium-containing salt substitutes" as a hyperkalaemia risk with ARBs (relevant in India where low-sodium salt with potassium chloride is promoted). Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
44	- D4-04-F08 | Losartan potassium and kidney advice (label) | Cozaar 5.4: "Monitor serum potassium periodically and treat appropriately. Dosage reduction or discontinuation of COZAAR may be required". Highlights: "Monitor renal function and potassium in susceptible patients." No numeric thresholds. RENAAL (1,513 type 2 diabetes with nephropathy): losartan cut sustained creatinine doubling by 25% and end-stage kidney disease by 29%, no effect on mortality. Year 2021 label. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=9949448f-c3b9-44ee-94ed-c1aca8c90f39 | label revised 2021-06 | OPENED | CITED
45	- D4-04-F09 | ARB low blood pressure: who is at risk | Telmisartan and losartan labels 5.2: symptomatic hypotension in patients with "an activated renin-angiotensin system, such as volume- or salt-depleted patients (e.g., those being treated with high doses of diuretics)". Mechanism: when salt and water are low, blood pressure leans on angiotensin II, so blocking it drops pressure more. Telmisartan label: dialysis patients "may develop orthostatic hypotension". A transient fall is not a contraindication. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
46	- D4-04-F10 | Telmisartan time course (label) | "Most of the antihypertensive effect is apparent within 2 weeks and maximal reduction is generally attained after 4 weeks." Response dose-related over 20 to 80 mg. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
47	- D4-04-F11 | Amlodipine ankle swelling: dose dependence and frequency | Norvasc label 6.1 placebo-controlled trials, edema: 1.8% at 2.5 mg (n=275), 3.0% at 5 mg (n=296), 10.8% at 10 mg (n=268), placebo 0.6% (n=520). So the step from 5 mg to 10 mg (protocol step 2) roughly triples edema (OUR ARITHMETIC: 10.8 / 3.0 = 3.6). Dizziness 1.1/3.4/3.4% vs 1.5%; flushing 0.7/1.4/2.6% vs 0.0%; palpitation 0.7/1.4/4.5% vs 0.6%. Pfizer SPL 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=abd6a2ca-40c2-485c-bc53-db1c652505ed | SPL 2025-06-09 | OPENED | CITED
48	- D4-04-F12 | Amlodipine edema is more common in women | Norvasc label: edema 5.6% in men and 14.6% in women on amlodipine (all doses pooled), against 1.4% and 5.1% on placebo (n=1,218 men, 512 women on drug). Pfizer SPL 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=abd6a2ca-40c2-485c-bc53-db1c652505ed | SPL 2025-06-09 | OPENED | CITED
49	- D4-04-F13 | Amlodipine: sudden low pressure unlikely, heart rate unchanged | Norvasc 5.1: "Because of the gradual onset of action, acute hypotension is unlikely." Chronic dosing lowers supine and standing pressure without significant change in heart rate or plasma catecholamines. 5.2: worsening angina or MI can follow starting or raising the dose in severe obstructive coronary disease. Pfizer SPL 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=abd6a2ca-40c2-485c-bc53-db1c652505ed | SPL 2025-06-09 | OPENED | CITED
50	- D4-04-F14 | Amlodipine in pregnancy (label) | Norvasc 8.1: post-marketing data "are not sufficient to inform a drug-associated risk for major birth defects and miscarriage"; no adverse developmental effects in animal studies. No boxed warning. Pfizer SPL 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=abd6a2ca-40c2-485c-bc53-db1c652505ed | SPL 2025-06-09 | OPENED | CITED
51	- D4-04-F15 | Chlorthalidone electrolytes (label) | Thalitone 5.3: can cause hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypochloraemic alkalosis, hypomagnesaemia; low magnesium makes low potassium "difficult to treat despite potassium repletion". "Monitor serum electrolytes periodically." Stop the drug if low potassium comes with muscle weakness, paresis or ECG changes. 12.2: "dose-related reductions in serum potassium levels, elevations in serum uric acid and blood glucose". No numeric thresholds or recheck interval. Label revised 12/2019. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=bc5a0299-115b-4e60-bb3f-c75a95c51c15 | label revised 2019-12, SPL 2026-06-26 | OPENED | CITED
52	- D4-04-F16 | Chlorthalidone uric acid, glucose, calcium (label) | Thalitone 5.4: may alter glucose tolerance; may raise cholesterol and triglycerides; raises uric acid "due to reduced clearance of uric acid" and may "precipitate gout in susceptible patients"; lowers urinary calcium so serum calcium can rise. Patient counselling lists signs of potassium loss: thirst, tiredness, drowsiness, restlessness, muscle cramps, nausea, vomiting, faster pulse. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=bc5a0299-115b-4e60-bb3f-c75a95c51c15 | label revised 2019-12 | OPENED | CITED
53	- D4-04-F17 | Chlorthalidone in pregnancy (label) | Thalitone 8.1: decades of observational data have not shown major birth defects or miscarriage, but "Chlorthalidone should not be used as first-line therapy to treat hypertension in pregnancy". Mechanism: thiazides cross the placenta (umbilical vein levels approach maternal plasma) and, like other diuretics, "can cause placental hypoperfusion"; neonatal jaundice, thrombocytopenia, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte problems reported. So the bar is softer than for ARBs (no boxed warning). https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=bc5a0299-115b-4e60-bb3f-c75a95c51c15 | label revised 2019-12 | OPENED | CITED
54	- D4-04-F18 | Chlorthalidone and the kidney, low pressure (label) | Thalitone 5.1-5.2: may cause symptomatic hypotension, more with impaired sympathetic response, volume depletion or salt restriction; diuretics can cause changes in renal function including acute renal failure, more in CKD, heart failure, volume depletion. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=bc5a0299-115b-4e60-bb3f-c75a95c51c15 | label revised 2019-12 | OPENED | CITED
55	- D4-04-F19 | Hydrochlorothiazide metabolic effects (label) | HCTZ label (Chartwell, rev. 07/2023): "Hyperuricemia may occur or acute gout may be precipitated"; "Hyperglycemia may occur with thiazide diuretics. Thus, latent diabetes mellitus may become manifest"; diabetics may need insulin or oral drug adjustment; raises urinary magnesium loss; may slightly raise serum calcium. Warning signs of fluid or electrolyte imbalance listed: dry mouth, thirst, weakness, lethargy, confusion, seizures, cramps, hypotension, oliguria, tachycardia. Orthostatic hypotension listed as an adverse reaction (worse with alcohol). https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=4e43dd27-3f4b-4205-a26e-6ecaa8281347 | label revised 2023-07 | OPENED | CITED
56	- D4-04-F20 | Hydrochlorothiazide in pregnancy (older-format label) | HCTZ label: "Routine use of diuretics during normal pregnancy is inappropriate and exposes mother and fetus to unnecessary hazard"; thiazides cross the placenta and appear in cord blood; risk of fetal or neonatal jaundice and thrombocytopenia. The same label also warns of non-melanoma skin cancer (sun protection) and acute angle-closure glaucoma within hours to weeks of starting. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=4e43dd27-3f4b-4205-a26e-6ecaa8281347 | label revised 2023-07 | OPENED | CITED
57	
58	### ARBs and the kidney: the creatinine rise, the 30% rule, when to recheck
59	
60	- D4-04-F21 | The 30% rule comes from Bakris and Weir 2000 | Review of 12 randomised trials (ACE inhibitor arms, n=1,102; average follow-up 3 years) in people with existing renal insufficiency: most showed an acute fall in GFR and rise in creatinine after starting. Conclusion: "acute increases in serum creatinine of up to 30% that stabilize within the first 2 months" of ACE-inhibitor therapy are strongly associated with long-term preservation of kidney function. Those with baseline creatinine 1.4 mg/dL or more had 55 to 75% risk reduction in renal progression. Note: ACE-inhibitor data, extended to ARBs by inference. Arch Intern Med 2000. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:10724055&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 10724055) | 2000-03 | OPENED | CITED
61	- D4-04-F22 | Disagreement: rises below 30% are not fully harmless (UK cohort) | Schmidt et al., BMJ 2017, UK CPRD 1997-2014, 122,363 people starting ACE inhibitor or ARB. 2,078 (1.7%) had creatinine rises of 30% or more; they were more often female, elderly, with heart or kidney disease, on NSAIDs, loop or potassium-sparing diuretics. Adjusted rate ratios for 30%+ rise against under 30%: end-stage renal disease 3.43 (2.40 to 4.91), MI 1.46 (1.16 to 1.84), heart failure 1.37 (1.14 to 1.65), death 1.84 (1.65 to 2.05). Graded: even 10-19% rise gave death IRR 1.15 (1.09 to 1.22) and 20-29% gave 1.35 (1.23 to 1.49) against under 10%. Observational, so the rise may mark sicker patients rather than cause harm. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:28279964&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 28279964, PMC5421447) | 2017-03 | OPENED | CITED
62	- D4-04-F23 | NICE NG203 recheck timing and thresholds for RAS blockers | NICE CKD guideline (published 25 Aug 2021, updated 24 Nov 2021), recs from 2008: 1.6.14 measure potassium and eGFR before starting and "between 1 and 2 weeks after starting renin-angiotensin system antagonists and after each dose increase". 1.6.19-1.6.20: do not change the dose if eGFR fall is under 25% or creatinine rise under 30%; repeat the test in 1 to 2 weeks. 1.6.21: if eGFR falls 25% or more or creatinine rises 30% or more, look for other causes (volume depletion, NSAIDs); if none, stop or reduce to a previously tolerated dose and add another drug. Scope: adults with CKD. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng203/chapter/Recommendations | 2021-11-24 | OPENED | CITED
63	- D4-04-F24 | NICE NG203 potassium thresholds for RAS blockers | 1.6.15: do not routinely start a RAS antagonist if pretreatment potassium "is greater than 5.0 mmol/litre". 1.6.18: stop RAS antagonists if potassium "increases to 6.0 mmol/litre or more" and other potassium-raising drugs have been stopped. 1.6.17: monitor more often if other potassium-raising drugs are co-prescribed. 1	# D4-05 Biomarkers and adherence signals (agent: claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-14)
2	
3	## Digest
4	
5	The 12 facts that matter most for the biology of the loop:
6	
7	1. By urine or blood drug assay, about 1 in 3 people with apparent resistant hypertension are not taking their drugs (pooled 31.2%, range 3% to 86%) (D4-05-F01); 25% to 42% in UK and Czech LC-MS/MS series (F02, F03).
8	2. In primary care it is far lower: 4.7% of older UK patients (F12). Belgian "resistant" referrals were mostly under-dosed, not non-adherent (F44).
9	3. Odds of non-adherence rise 77% to 85% per added drug (F03; OR 1.57 in Brazil, F07). Each step-up raises the risk.
10	4. Self-report fails: 90.1% adherent by questionnaire vs 32.4% by urine assay (F07). In India, 99DOTS phone self-report had sensitivity 70%, NPV 21% against urine tests (F23).
11	5. Feeding assay results back raised adherence (70% to 92.5%) but did not lower BP in two RCTs (RHYME F05; OUTREACH -5.1 mmHg, NS, F11). Big BP falls come only from uncontrolled before-after data (F04).
12	6. Amlodipine and telmisartan leave no pulse signature (F16, F18); beta-blockers do (F41), diltiazem slightly (F42).
13	7. ARBs raise renin (losartan 2 to 3 times, F19); a 48% fall in aldosterone-to-renin ratio from baseline flagged adherence with 90% sensitivity, 75% specificity (one 40-patient study, F43).
14	8. Chlorthalidone lowers potassium and raises uric acid, dose-related and in step with its BP effect (F21, F22): a weak intake sign.
15	9. Recheck creatinine and potassium 2 to 4 weeks after starting or raising an ARB; continue unless creatinine rises over 30% (KDIGO 2024, F27, F28). eGFR change over 20% (F29) or ACR doubling (F33) is beyond noise.
16	10. HbA1c moves over 2 to 3 months; it cannot judge a 30-day step (F37).
17	11. India's free public list: dipstick at village level; creatinine, urea, uric acid at PHC; potassium and urine ACR sent to a hub; NT-proBNP only at district level (F39).
18	12. Long half-lives blur single assays: amlodipine 30 to 50 h (F17), chlorthalidone 40 to 60 h (F21); a dose just before a test hides gaps (Hawthorne effect, F06).
19	
20	Surprises: cheap reminder devices did nothing in a 53,480-person RCT (F24), but reminder packaging raised pills taken 11% (F46); no Indian drug-assay study for hypertension exists that we found (F15); a smartphone home urine ACR test is FDA-cleared (F49).
21	
22	Against lead 1: non-adherence grows with each added drug (F03), and objective adherence feedback has not yet lowered BP in RCTs (F05, F11).
23	
24	## What this suggests for the product
25	
26	- Suggestion: before any step-up, use signals beyond the patient's word, but do not expect a cheap body signal for the protocol drugs: amlodipine and telmisartan leave no pulse change (F16, F18). Pill counts or photos of the strip and refill dates are the practical first layer (F46, F47, F48).
27	- Suggestion: weight the adherence question by the number of drugs; risk rises about 1.8 times per added drug (F03, F07), so steps 3 to 5 need a stronger check than steps 1 to 2.
28	- Suggestion: borrow the Lane trigger as a rule: if systolic falls less than 10 mmHg after a new drug is added, flag possible non-adherence before the next step (F14).
29	- Suggestion: schedule creatinine and potassium 2 to 4 weeks after telmisartan starts or doubles, with a 30% creatinine-rise rule for doctor review (F27, F28); this fits inside the 30-day cycle.
30	- Suggestion: at chlorthalidone start, a baseline and 2 to 4 week potassium and uric acid gives both a safety check and a weak sign of intake (F21, F22). Potassium needs a hub sample in the public system (F39).
31	- Suggestion: do not use HbA1c or NT-proBNP as step-cycle signals; HbA1c is a 3-monthly check (F37); NT-proBNP is district-level and ₹1,200 to ₹3,520 privately (F35, F36), for suspected heart failure only.
32	- Suggestion: treat a drug assay as a referral-level test, not a loop feature: no Indian assay service or price was found (F15, NOT FOUND below), and RCT benefit on BP is unproven (F05, F11).
33	- Suggestion: if the loop wants an ARB-specific lab sign, a baseline renin or aldosterone-to-renin ratio before telmisartan and a repeat at 2 weeks is the only tested option found (F43); evidence is one 40-patient study.

1	## 2. What the research found
2	
3	Chapter 1 showed a large, treatable population, a system that loses half of it between visits, and a market that stops before the dose. This chapter condenses what the research found, in plain words. It starts with the clinical evidence on what actually improves outcomes, then turns to how others have scaled care without specialists, what the technology can and cannot do, who is already doing this, where the money is and what the rules allow.
4	
5	### 2.1 What actually improves outcomes
6	
7	> **In short.**
8	> - Outcomes improved when a home reading led to a changed treatment, and mostly did not when the reading was only shown or turned into a reminder.
9	> - Who was allowed to change the dose mattered more than the electronics.
10	> - Raising adherence on its own did not move outcomes.
11	> - The same pattern holds in diabetes, heart failure, warfarin and asthma, and the known harms of dose stepping can be met with stop rules.
12	
13	The trials sort into five rules. OUR VIEW: the sorting is ours; the numbers are from the notes.
14	
15	**Rule 1. The reading must change the treatment.** Across 15 pooled trials (7,138 people, 12 months), self-monitoring of blood pressure alone lowered systolic pressure (the upper number, in mmHg, millimetres of mercury) by 1.0 mmHg against usual care: no effect. With intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling), not dose changes alone, it fell 6.1 mmHg [D1-01-F05]. Where the dose itself moved, the falls were larger. In the UK trial TASMIN-SR (552 high-risk patients, randomised, meaning people got each treatment by chance), patients stepping their own dose by an agreed plan had systolic pressure 9.2 mmHg lower than under usual care at 12 months [D1-01-F02]. In the US trial HyperLink (450 patients, 16 clinics randomised as clusters, meaning whole clinics rather than single patients), pharmacists adjusting drugs from home readings got 57.2% controlled against 30.0% with usual care [D1-01-F04]. An independent US review by the Peterson Health Technology Institute (PHTI, October 2024) rated monitoring-only programmes "not clinically meaningful" and programmes where care teams adjust drugs "clinically meaningful and more rapid", against a threshold of a 5 mmHg fall in systolic pressure [D1-01-F39].
16	
17	![Extra fall in systolic pressure against usual care, by what was done with the reading](adaptive-care-pictures/20-what-lowers-pressure.png)
18	
19	*Chart: separate trials with different patients and end points, so compare the groups, not single bars [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F02, D1-01-F03, D1-01-F04, D1-01-F05, D1-01-F06, D1-01-F07].*
20	
21	**Rule 2. Who is allowed to decide matters more than the electronics.** In the UK trial TASMINH4 (1,182 patients, 12 months), the family doctor adjusted doses in every arm, and sending home readings electronically instead of on paper added 1.2 mmHg, not significant (small enough to be chance) [D1-01-F03]. In rural China, the China Rural Hypertension Control Project (CRHCP: 326 villages, 33,995 people aged 40 and over) let village doctors start and step drugs by a standard protocol under physician supervision. At 18 months, 57.0% were under 130/80 against 19.9% with enhanced usual care [D1-01-F09]. After a median of 4 years, cardiovascular events were lower, with a hazard ratio (a risk ratio over time; below 1 means fewer events) of 0.75 at age 60 and over and 0.64 under 60. The programme also gave free or discounted drugs and paid village doctors incentives tied to control rates, so the effect cannot be credited to the protocol alone [D1-01-F38].
22	
23	India has the null result that belongs here. mWellcare (40 community health centres, 3,698 people with hypertension, diabetes or both, 12 months, randomised by centre) gave nurses and doctors an app that prompted treatment steps during visits. Against enhanced usual care the systolic difference was 0.98 mmHg, not significant; both arms fell by about 13 mmHg [D1-01-F46]. OUR VIEW: it shows that a prompt at a visit adds nothing to a well-run protocol programme. It does not show that dose changes between visits fail: the app did not act on home readings or reach patients who never came back, and no Indian randomised trial of home readings driving a dose protocol was found (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
24	
25	![Share of patients under control with and without a programme that steps the dose](adaptive-care-pictures/21-share-controlled.png)
26	
27	*Chart: three settings where someone other than a specialist was allowed to step the dose. The China programme also gave free or cheaper medicines and paid for results; the India figures are before and after among the 51% who returned, with no comparison group [D1-01-F04, D1-01-F09, D1-03-F10].*
28	
29	**Rule 3. Adherence technology alone does not move outcomes.** Smart pillboxes or medication labels for tuberculosis (ASCENT, 23,483 patients, four countries) did not reduce poor outcomes against standard care [D1-02-F59]. Inhaler reminders for 220 New Zealand children raised adherence to 84% against 30% over 6 months, with no difference in school absence [D1-02-F01]. A blood-pressure reminder app (MedISAFE-BP, 411 US adults, 12 weeks) moved systolic pressure by 0.5 mmHg, not significant [D1-01-F06]. OUR VIEW: raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, so adherence is an input to the dose decision, not a product.
30	
31	**Rule 4. Someone must pay for the outcome.** Chapter 1.5 told this side: apps and sensors sold on their own failed, while the firms that lasted are paid by employers and insurers, or sell a device that delivers the therapy.
32	
33	**Rule 5. People stay when their own clinician is in it.** In eight remote US studies (over 1,00,000 participants), median retention was 5.5 days; referral by a clinician added 40 days, and payment 22 days (one study) [D1-02-F27]. OUR VIEW: a consumer app is the wrong shape.
34	
35	#### What the loop changes, by kind
36	
37	| What the loop changes | Home signal | Proof | Who decides |
38	|---|---|---|---|
39	| 1. Drug dose or protocol step | Cuff, fasting sugar, INR (a blood test of clotting time), weight | Strong | Patient on an agreed plan, pharmacist, nurse or health worker |
40	| 2. Food and behaviour | Glucose sensor, step count | Mixed | App, coach |
41	| 3. Exercise as the dose | Camera, pulse, effort rating | Matches in-person care | Therapist or app |
42	| 4. Therapy delivered by the device (closed-loop insulin pump) | Glucose sensor | Strong | Algorithm, within limits a clinician sets [D1-05-F41] |
43	| 5. Biofeedback (a body signal shown back to the patient) | Breathing or pulse sensor | Weak | Patient |
44	
45	OUR VIEW: proof is strongest in kinds 1 and 4, where a drug dose with a known effect is changed and the signal is cheap, valid and fast. Kind 4 needs expensive hardware; kind 1 needs almost none.

57	Other areas repeat the pattern. Nurses stepping gout drugs to a target worked with no software at all [D1-02-F06]; tele-rehabilitation matches in-person care but does not beat usual care [D1-02-F03, D1-02-F07]; and guided breathing for blood pressure showed no effect once maker-linked trials were removed [D1-02-F11].
58	
59	**Prescription apps and safety.** Software sold as a prescribed treatment has passed trials, yet most of the companies behind it failed (chapter 1.5), and none of the prescription apps in the research note changes a drug dose. The closest, Japan's CureApp HT, coaches lifestyle: in 390 untreated adults over 12 weeks it lowered 24-hour systolic pressure 2.4 mmHg more than lifestyle advice alone [D1-01-F07]. OUR VIEW: dose stepping by protocol has a good safety record when the protocol has stop rules. At 4 years in rural China, injurious falls, symptomatic low blood pressure, fainting and kidney outcomes did not differ between groups [D1-01-F38], and insulin-dose proposals in TeleDiab-2 (191 adults, 4 months) caused no severe low blood sugar [D1-01-F14]. The known costs, more minor side effects, leg swelling and low blood sugar, each need their own safety branch.
60	
61	### 2.2 How care has been scaled without specialists
62	
63	> **In short.**
64	> - India's programme already has a protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list; the dose step still waits for a doctor's visit.
65	> - Patients who keep attending do well on the protocol; the loss is among those who stop coming.
66	> - Abroad, the largest gains came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill.
67	> - Software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.
68	
69	Chapter 2.1 showed that changing the dose works. This section asks how it has been delivered at scale without specialists.
70	
71	#### India's hypertension programme in practice
72	
73	IHCI runs a state protocol of 3 to 4 steps, amlodipine first (chapter 4.1 gives one state's steps); Punjab and Maharashtra order the steps differently at the second step [D3-05-F01, D1-06-F01, D1-06-F02]. Drugs are free, as 30-day refills at every facility level from health and wellness centres to district hospitals [D3-05-F02]. The open-source Simple app takes about 80 seconds to register a patient and 15 seconds for a follow-up, lists overdue patients with high-risk ones first, and offers one-click nurse calls and automated reminders [D3-05-F03]. Medical officers start amlodipine and review at 30 days; nurses register patients and record follow-up [D3-05-F06].
74	
75	For patients who keep coming, the protocol works: in Punjab and Maharashtra, 70% and 76% of patients seen again were controlled on amlodipine 5 mg alone, and 75% and 81% after step 2 [D3-05-F04]. Across 159,292 patients who returned and stayed on protocol, control on clinic readings plateaued at 77% and 82%; about 43% of starters are missing from that count [D1-06-F04]. The drugs are cheap: amlodipine for the first two steps cut drug cost about 20%, from US$2.50 to US$2.05 per patient per year, not counting staff [D3-05-F05].
76	
77	OUR VIEW: IHCI already has the protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list. It lacks a dose decision for the uncontrolled patient who does not go back to the doctor (chapter 1.3).
78	
79	**Who changes the dose in practice.** Besides the refill rule in chapter 1.3, search summaries (only) say that state protocol text has the medical officer start and raise the dose, while the ANM (auxiliary nurse midwife) gives a month's medicines once pressure is controlled [D3-05-F31], and that a CHO (community health officer) screens, refers and follows up [D3-05-F30, D3-05-F13]. Whether a nurse or health officer may change a dose in law is open (chapter 2.6). OUR VIEW: design for a doctor approving every dose change.
80	
81	**Tamil Nadu's doorstep scheme.** Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam, launched in August 2021, reported 1,86,13,872 beneficiaries by August 2024, with 92,59,821 people with hypertension given medicines (government figures, not audited; THEIR CLAIM) [D3-05-F14]. It refills; it does not step: no source says the dose is changed at the door [D3-05-F15]. OUR VIEW: high treatment with low control (chapter 1.2) is the gap a dose step addresses.
82

94	OUR VIEW: the largest gains in control came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill; monitoring, counselling or prompts gained less or nothing. What these programmes changed, and software alone could not, was drug stock, authority for a non-doctor to change drugs (the PAHO HEARTS roadmap across 33 countries names nurse dose adjustment [D3-05-F28]), a person carrying medicine home, pay linked to control, and a person who phones and books visits. Software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.
95	
96	### 2.3 What the technology can and cannot do
97	
98	> **In short.**
99	> - A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons unrelated to the cuff, such as posture; trusting it is the hard engineering.
100	> - Every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing.
101	> - Language models make dose errors even when told to follow a protocol; they can read and speak, but should not decide.
102	> - Learning each patient's response is later work: no open data or simulator exists for blood-pressure drugs.
103	
104	If changing the treatment is what works, the technology questions narrow to two: can a home reading be trusted, and can a decision be kept within safe bounds. OUR VIEW: the hard engineering is in trusting the home reading and in bounding the decision, not in the model that makes it.
105	
106	#### Trusting a home reading
107	
108	The American and European hypertension societies publish rules for home readings: how long to rest, how many readings, over how many days, and a lower threshold at home than in clinic; chapter 4.3 applies them [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F11, D2-01-F1]. Small mistakes move the number:
109	
110	| Mistake | Effect, systolic / diastolic (mmHg) |
111	|---|---|
112	| Arm on the lap instead of on a desk | +3.9 / +4.0 (randomised crossover trial, 133 people, Baltimore) [D2-02-F16] |
113	| Arm hanging at the side | +6.5 / +4.4 (same trial) |
114	| Back not supported; legs crossed | +5 to +15 / +6; +5 to +8 / +3 to +5 (American Heart Association) [D2-02-F18] |
115	| Regular cuff on an arm that needs a large or an extra-large one | +4.8 or +19.5 systolic (randomised crossover trial, 195 people) [D2-02-F19] |
116	
117	Noise has already hurt an Indian trial. SMARThealth India (a stepped-wedge cluster trial, in which groups of patients start the programme one after another; 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh) found no blood-pressure effect, partly because "fluctuating BP values" made risk scores disagree, so only 37.2% of the cohort was exposed [D2-03-F17].
118	
119	Getting the number in is also hard. No cuff sold in India was confirmed to use the standard Bluetooth blood-pressure service [D2-02-F3]. A purpose-trained reader of cuff-screen photos reached mean errors of 1.2/0.8 mmHg on 776 US images, but 82% of 7,205 images in a Guatemalan set were poor quality, and only Omron screens were tested [D2-02-F4]. No published test of a general vision-language model on these screens was found [D2-02-F8]. A Bluetooth home cuff, the Omron HEM-7156T, costs about ₹2,600 (2026 listings ₹2,593-3,500; search summary only) [D1-06-F31]. Cuffless blood pressure is not ready: the FDA cleared one cuffless monitor in July 2025 [D2-02-F23], but the European Society of Hypertension says there are "no generally accepted protocols" for validating such devices [D2-02-F25].
120	
121	OUR VIEW: blood pressure is the one signal a household can measure with a validated, cheap device. Cuffless error is about the size of a dose step, so dose decisions stay on cuff readings, and every photo read must be shown back to the patient to confirm.
122	
123	#### Algorithms that set a dose
124	
125	Every dose algorithm in use is bounded. The do-it-yourself insulin system OpenAPS writes its safety rules down: it acts only through temporary basal rates, so if it stops, the pump returns to the normal plan; the rate is capped by the lowest of several limits, including "4x the current scheduled basal rate"; and missing or conflicting data sends it back to the pre-set plan [D2-03-F46]. The American Diabetes Association's 2025 insulin rule steps the dose every 3 days towards a fasting target and lowers it 10-20% after an unexplained low [D1-06-F16]; India's ICMR workflow gives targets but no titration schedule [D1-06-F17]. Blood-pressure ladders use fixed steps with a 30-day review, lab and pregnancy guards and referral at the end (chapter 4.1) [D1-06-F14].
126	
127	People do differ. PHYSIC (randomised, double-blind, repeated crossover, 280 people, Sweden) found real between-person differences in drug response, worth about 4.4 mmHg if the drug were chosen per person [D2-03-F12], while a one-time "responder" label did not predict 12-month response in 608 Chinese patients [D2-03-F13]. OUR VIEW: every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing; a ladder is the simplest case, and PHYSIC is the honest reason a later learning layer could add value.
128	
129	#### A protocol as data, and decision support in India
130	
131	A protocol written as data, not code, can be read by a clinician, tested branch by branch and swapped without changing the engine. No ready standard fits: WHO SMART Guidelines have no general hypertension kit [D2-03-F50]. Testing is the hard part: when the US VA re-encoded its hypertension decision support (ATHENA-HTN), 26 decision points gave 3,120 possible outputs, and 100 test cases covered "only 1% of the possible output combinations" [D2-03-F55].
132	
133	Indian trials of decision support for clinicians are mixed. CARRS (chapter 2.2) was positive with care coordinators; mWellcare (chapter 2.1) [D2-03-F15] and SMARThealth (above) were null. IMPACT Diabetes (cluster randomised, 418 people, 9 months) gave ASHAs (village health workers) a tablet tool under physician supervision: HbA1c fell by 0.5 or more in 21.8% against 10.3% with usual care [D2-03-F18, D3-04-F17]. OUR VIEW: decision support alone did not beat a well-run programme in two Indian trials, so an engine must act between visits, not prompt during them, and ATHENA's 1% says to test on generated cases and replayed data, not only hand-written ones.
134	
135	#### What language models may and may not do with doses
136	
137	GPT-4, prompted with a hospital tacrolimus protocol on 300 simulated cases, made 13.9% "sentinel errors" in its first version; with stronger constraints and output checks the rate fell to 1.0%, and 13.3% of runs were not reproducible (OUR ARITHMETIC: 100 - 86.7) [D2-03-F38]. No completed randomised trial of a language-model coach with a blood-pressure or HbA1c outcome was found; two are registered [D2-03-F44]. Of the health models the large labs have built, only MedGemma, PaPaGei and HealthBench can be downloaded, and none sets doses [D2-03-F32, D2-03-F28, D2-03-F33].
138	
139	OUR VIEW, following [D2-03-F38, D2-03-F40, D2-03-F46]: the model handles language only (reading the cuff photo, translation, speech); a fixed, tested engine makes every decision from the protocol file; code checks every output against the protocol; and a clinician approves every change.
140	
141	#### Later work
142	
143	Adaptive nudging, which learns when and what to send each person, has one head-to-head win, on steps, not on a clinical measure (DIAMANTE, 168 people, US) [D2-03-F10]. A "digital twin" (a model of one person that predicts their response) is further off for blood-pressure drugs. No open model of that response, no titration simulator, no open type 2 diabetes simulator and no large open dataset of home readings with medicine changes was found [D1-06-F42, D1-06-F43, D1-06-F30]. What can be tested on now is the programme's control-by-step figures [D1-06-F04] and open home blood-pressure series (the R `bp` package, GPL-3) [D2-03-F61]. OUR VIEW: each approved step in a loop gives one labelled example, readings before and 30 days after, which is the dataset a response model would need.
144

191	
192	### 2.5 The money
193	
194	> **In short.**
195	> - Most money in blood-pressure care goes to medicines; a service priced near a pill would double the patient's bill, so usually someone else must pay.
196	> - No Indian payer was found for remote monitoring or digital therapy; our view is that a private clinic or hospital chain is the likeliest first payer.
197	> - On our own arithmetic the reachable Indian market is real but small for a venture fund, and the US$100 million-a-year test fails on India alone.
198	> - Indian chronic-care firms in the notes lose money; the profitable foreign ones are paid by employers and plans.
199	
200	Chapter 1.5 showed who pays today. This section follows the rupee further.
201	
202	#### What is spent today
203	
204	India's retail medicine market was ₹2,45,943 crore in the year to March 2026 [D2-05-F02]. Blood-pressure medicines sold about ₹16,371 crore at retail chemists in the year to December 2025 (not hospital tenders or Jan Aushadhi; the page does not label the period explicitly) [D2-05-F01]. One amlodipine plus telmisartan 5/40 pill a day had a median price of ₹10.7 a tablet for a private brand, ₹1.5 for a Jan Aushadhi generic and ₹0.59 in the public programme (2019-20 prices). The private brand comes to about ₹3,906 a year, about ₹325 a month (OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹10.7 x 365); that is the cost of one brand pill, not a measured patient spend, and the paper's private range is about ₹2,500-5,100 a year [D2-05-F17]. No measured public-private split of treatment was found; a 2021 letter assumed 30% public [D2-05-F30]. OUR VIEW: a service near the price of one combination pill doubles the bill, so usually someone else must pay.
205	
206	#### Who could pay in India
207	
208	| Payer | What the notes have | Would they pay (OUR VIEW) |
209	|---|---|---|
210	| Patients | Chapter 1.5 | Some urban patients will; a monthly fee on top of medicines is hard for most |
211	| Clinics and hospital chains | The private sector gives about 70% of all outpatient care (authors' statement, 2021) [D3-07-F03] | Yes, if the loop keeps patients and refills inside their system |
212	| Medicine makers | Patient-support budgets NOT FOUND [D2-05-F40] | Possible, but a maker that sells the drug being stepped up has a conflict |
213	| Insurers | IRDAI's 2024 master circular says insurers should offer chronic and outpatient cover but does not mandate it [D2-04-F33] | Not yet: almost no outpatient cover |
214	| Employers | Could not be confirmed | Possible, with a slow sales cycle |
215	| States | Chapters 1.3 and 1.5; AB-PMJAY pays for hospital care only (search summary only) [D2-04-F47] | Largest pool, lowest price; only for proven results |

236	#### The US$100 million-a-year test
237	
238	US$100 million a year is ₹942 crore at ₹94.25 to the dollar (rate on 13 Nov 2026). At ₹1,788 a patient a year that needs 52.7 lakh paying patients, more than the SAM holds. **On this model the test fails in India alone**: it needs 1.3 times the SAM (all OUR ARITHMETIC). Price moves the result as much as clinic count: at ₹99 a month the SAM used is ₹498 crore and 79.3 lakh patients are needed; at ₹299 it is ₹1,504 crore and 26.3 lakh; at Omada's revenue of about US$24.5 a member a month, 3,40,136 patients would do [D2-05-F23]. A public tier, shown apart, at ₹15 a month (ASSUMPTION) for the public programme's hypertension patients (chapter 1.3) would come to ₹756 crore a year (OUR ARITHMETIC), but a state would pay it only for results. OUR VIEW: blood pressure in India is the entry, not the whole company; the rest must come from more protocols on the same loop, a paid public tier, other countries or a higher price paid by an insurer, employer or medicine maker.
239	
240	#### Unit economics, per patient a month
241	
242	Every line is an ASSUMPTION from the build note. The clinic pays ₹149 (below Sugar.fit's ₹2,499 a month; OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹29,990 / 12). Costs are messages ₹15, cloud ₹5, reading cuff photos ₹2, and a health-worker call to silent patients ₹30, so the gross margin is ₹149 - 52 = ₹97, about 65% (OUR ARITHMETIC). Doctor time comes to about 4 minutes per 100 patients a month (6.5-8.5 proposals at 30 seconds each; OUR SIMULATION and ASSUMPTION), not costed. OUR VIEW: the health-worker call is the largest cost, and the margin holds only if doctors approve proposals without being paid per approval.
243	
244	#### Comparable companies and the funding climate
245	
246	Indian chronic-care firms in the notes lose money: Sugar.fit had revenue of ₹66.5 crore in FY25 and a loss of ₹42 crore [D2-05-F19]; Healthify had revenue of ₹228.76 crore in FY23 and a loss of ₹142 crore (aggregators) [D2-05-F22]. Abroad, Omada's revenue per member is US$294 a year (the monthly figure used above; OUR ARITHMETIC: 294 / 12), at a 76% gross margin [D2-05-F23], and no US medicine-adjusting programme publishes a price per member a month. US digital health raised US$7.4 billion in H1 2026 [D2-05-F16]; Indian health-tech raised US$310 million (headline only, tracker not named) [D2-05-F11].
247	
248	OUR VIEW: Omada's level of revenue a member is reached abroad only with employer and insurer payers. Indian comparables are small and loss-making.
249	
250	### 2.6 The rules
251	
252	> **In short.**
253	> - India's July 2026 guidance treats software that guides treatment as a medical device; a doctor-approved dose proposal could fall in Class A, B or C, which the regulator confirms.
254	> - In telemedicine, only a registered doctor may prescribe, and must deliver the prescription directly.
255	> - A study on patients needs permission and ethics approval first.
256	> - Abroad, each country pays through a clinician, and Germany ties part of the price to results.
257	
258	These are readings of the texts; open points remain questions for a lawyer and for CDSCO, India's medical-device regulator.
259	
260	#### Software as a medical device
261	
262	CDSCO issued its "Guidance Document on Medical Device Software" on 21 Jul 2026 [D2-04-F01]. India has four risk classes, A lowest and D highest, and the class follows the intended use stated in the label, website and promotion [D2-04-F02]. The grid for standalone software [D2-04-F03]:
263	
264	| Situation | Treatment or diagnosis | Drive clinical management | Inform clinical management |
265	|---|---|---|---|
266	| Critical | D | C | B |
267	| Serious | C | B | A |
268	| Non-serious | B | A | A |
269	
270	"Drive clinical management" covers information "to guide next diagnostics or next treatment interventions" [D2-04-F04]. A dose proposal that a doctor approves reads most naturally as "drive": Class B if hypertension is "serious", Class A if "non-serious", Class C if CDSCO reads it as "treatment" [D2-04-F06, D2-04-F49]. The guidance does not say where hypertension sits [D2-04-F05], and a patient-facing tool used without a professional can be moved up to "critical". CDSCO names a hypertension digital-therapeutics platform as medical device software [D2-04-F07], and India has no exemption for tools only a clinician sees [D2-04-F10]. OUR VIEW: clinician sign-off lowers the class; it does not take the software out of the device rules.
271	
272	#### Testing on patients
273	
274	A test licence (Form MD-13) covers making small quantities "for the purpose of Clinical Investigations or Test or Evaluation or Demonstration" [D2-04-F13]. A clinical investigation on patients needs CDSCO permission (MD-22/MD-23) [D2-04-F14], which the flowchart says is not mandatory for Class A [D2-04-F39]. Whether a pilot in which software drafts and a doctor decides counts as one is a question for counsel [D2-04-F50]. Trials must be registered on CTRI before the first patient, with ethics approval uploaded; whether a pilot in which the clinician decides needs this was NOT FOUND (search summary only) [D2-04-F45]. Fees and processing days were NOT FOUND [D2-04-F16].
275	
276	#### Who may prescribe and change a dose
277	
278	The Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (25 Mar 2020), clause 5.4, say platforms based on artificial intelligence or machine learning "are not allowed to counsel the patients or prescribe any medicines"; they may "assist and support" the doctor, but only a registered doctor may counsel or prescribe, and "the final prescription or counseling has to be directly delivered by the RMP" (registered medical practitioner) [D2-04-F17]. Whether later rules changed this in 2026 was not checked. In the national hypertension programme, community health officers delivered refills "based on the patient's prior prescription", and no law, rule or ministry order was found that lets a nurse, health officer or pharmacist change a dose under a standing order [D2-04-F18]. The Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954 bans advertisements suggesting a drug treats "High or low blood pressure", among other listed conditions; whether software counts as a "drug" under it is untested [D2-04-F31].
279	
280	OUR VIEW, for tonight's prototype: it is for test and demonstration, not a device on sale and not tested on patients; it uses open data, simulated patients or teammates' readings; a clinician approves every change and delivers the prescription, while the software only drafts; and it makes no claim that it treats or controls high blood pressure.
281	
282	#### Rules and payment abroad
283	
284	| Country | Device rule | How it is paid |
285	|---|---|---|
286	| United States | Insulin-titration software is a Class II device cleared by 510(k), for example My Dose Coach and d-Nav [D2-04-F24]; whether clinician-facing software that uses home cuff readings is a device at all is a question for counsel [D2-04-F22, D2-04-F23] | Medicare remote monitoring needs a face-to-face initiating visit from 1 Jan 2027 [D2-04-F26] |
287	| Germany | The DiGA route requires a positive care effect, with a decision in 3 months [D2-04-F28] | From 1 Jan 2026 at least 20% of the price must depend on measured outcomes [D2-04-F29, D1-05-F31] |
288	| Japan | CureApp HT, approved in April 2022 (search summary only), has been insured since 1 Sep 2022 as an add-on app that coaches lifestyle, not a dose change [D3-06-F19, D2-04-F37] | From 1 Jun 2026, 90 points a month in person or 78 online, plus 7,010 yen for the app (company release and a news report); the patient pays 30% (search summary only) [D2-04-F43, D3-06-F20]. Older figures differ: 7,010 yen (Jan 2024) or about 2,490 yen a month at a 30% patient share (2022), on different bases, unreconciled [D1-05-F33]; about 8,000 yen (search summary only) [D1-01-F57] |
289	
290	OUR VIEW: all three pay through a clinician, and Germany now ties part of the price to outcomes.
291	
292	Full detail: Appendix B (the clinical evidence and the programmes), Appendix C (the technology), Appendix D (every player) and Appendix E (money and rules).
293	
294	OUR VIEW: the research points one way. The treatment change, made by someone allowed to make it, is what works. India's programme has everything for it except a decision between visits. The technology to trust a home reading and bound a decision exists in open parts. No Indian service was found that does it, and no payer was found for it. The next chapter puts these findings together and weighs what to build.
295

1	## 4. The product we can build
2	
3	Chapter 3 ended with a choice: the home blood-pressure step loop. This chapter shows that product end to end: what it does, what the patient and the doctor see, and the checks that stop a bad reading or a missed tablet from changing a dose. It ends with the same loop carrying other protocols.
4	
5	### 4.1 What it does
6	
7	OUR DESIGN. The loop is for adults on blood-pressure medicine who miss the 30-day review: the half who do not return (chapter 1.3). Once a month the patient takes a week of home readings with an upper-arm cuff and sends each one as a photo of the cuff's screen. The software checks the readings, asks whether the medicine was taken, and drafts the next step of the state's published protocol, with its reasons. A registered doctor approves, edits or rejects it in one tap, and the patient gets the change in their own language, in the doctor's name. Nothing that changes treatment reaches the patient before a clinician approves.
8	
9	The protocol is Gujarat's published ladder: amlodipine 5 mg, then 10 mg, then add telmisartan 40 mg, then raise it to 80 mg, then add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg if chlorthalidone is not available), with a re-check after 30 days on each step. After the last step the sheet says: "Check if the patient has been taking medications regularly and correctly. If yes, refer to a specialist." It covers adults over 30. Its safety rules are in chapter 4.7, and every protocol rule in this chapter comes from that sheet [D1-06-F14].
10	
11	### 4.2 The system map
12	
13	A loop that changes treatment has six stages. Open parts already exist for each (Appendix C); the work is joining them with a safety rule at each handover (OUR VIEW).
14	
15	| Stage | Its job | Our build tonight (OUR VIEW) |
16	|---|---|---|
17	| Sense | Get a number from the home | Photo of any cuff's screen, confirmed by the patient; typed entry as fallback |
18	| Check | Was the reading taken properly | Kit-built motion clip plus a phone checklist |
19	| Decide | Turn valid readings into a proposed step | One file per protocol, run by one `decide()` function |
20	| Confirm | A clinician accepts or rejects | Clinician queue: Approve, Edit, Reject |
21	| Act | Tell the patient, in their language | Telegram chat plus a web form |
22	| Learn | Improve choices from each response | Roadmap only; nothing learns tonight |
23	
24	![System map of the step loop](adaptive-care-pictures/14-system-map.png)
25	
26	*The six stages of the loop and the technology chosen for each tonight.*
27	
28	The engine is one pure Python function, `decide()` (OUR DESIGN). It reads a protocol file written in YAML (a plain-text data format), the patient's state and the week's readings, and returns a proposal with its reasons. It never computes a dose: it can only pick a regimen written in the file. Each number in the file carries the sheet's own words; a value the source does not give is left blank, and the engine refuses that branch until a clinician fills it. No language model sits in the dose path (chapter 2.3 gives the reason); a model only reads the cuff photo and handles translation and speech.
29	
30	### 4.3 The patient side
31	
32	![Patient chat on the phone](adaptive-care-pictures/10-bp-patient-chat.png)
33	
34	*Mock-up with example data.*
35	
36	The patient uses a Telegram chat, or a web form if the chat fails, on a phone that may be a family member's (chapter 1.3). It prompts a measurement, takes a photo or typed reading, asks about tablets and delivers the change.
37	
38	The home-reading rule (OUR DESIGN, from published guidance): on days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle the patient takes two readings 1 minute apart after 5 minutes of seated rest, morning before tablets and evening [D2-02-F10]. A session counts only if both readings pass the quality checks. The engine needs at least 3 valid days and aims for 7, as the European Society of Hypertension advises; the same society says a home mean of 135/85 corresponds to 140/90 in clinic [D2-01-F1]; the International Society of Hypertension [D2-01-F3] and the Indian Guidelines IV (search summary only) [D2-01-F4] use the same home line. So a mean at or above 135 systolic or 85 diastolic is "still high"; one session at or above 180 or 110 is "very high".
39	
40	The Gujarat sheet is written for clinic readings at 140/90. **Applying a clinic protocol to home readings at 135/85 is OUR DESIGN.** The team says so aloud on the slide, and the threshold stays a value the clinician signs. No Indian home-against-clinic offset was searched.
41	
42	The photo is read twice by a vision model, checked against plausible ranges and shown back for the person to confirm; memory screens are rejected. General vision models are untested on cuff screens (chapter 2.3) [D2-02-F8]. A photo cannot prove who measured or when; the clip's time-stamped record (chapter 4.5) narrows that gap without closing it. Typed entry is always built; Bluetooth only if an Omron HEM-7156T is in hand [D2-02-F1].
43	
44	### 4.4 The doctor side
45	
46	![Clinician queue of proposal cards](adaptive-care-pictures/11-bp-doctor-queue.png)
47	
48	*Mock-up with example data.*
49	
50	The doctor sees a queue of cards, urgent ones first, batched once a day. Each card shows the current step, a 7-day sparkline (a small chart of the week's readings), the mean, the answer to the medicine question, the protocol line it quotes, the safety checks ticked and the proposed regimen, with Approve, Edit and Reject. A timer logs each decision. Because the card carries everything needed, the decision is one tap (OUR DESIGN).
51	
52	![One proposal card in detail](adaptive-care-pictures/12-bp-doctor-detail.png)
53	
54	*Mock-up with example data.*
55	
56	The approval and the patient message are the doctor's own act, sent in the doctor's name: OUR DESIGN, and a question for a lawyer, since the telemedicine guidelines want the registered doctor to deliver the prescription directly (chapter 2.6).
57	
58	### 4.5 Trusting the reading
59	
60	A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons unrelated to the cuff, such as an arm hanging at the side (chapter 2.3). The loop answers with a small clip built from the maker kit (OUR DESIGN): an ESP32 board with two MPU6050 motion sensors, one on the cuff and one on the forearm. A helper seats the person correctly once, and the clip stores that posture. It then enforces 300 seconds of still rest, restarting on movement; checks that the forearm is within 20 degrees of flat (a hanging arm fails) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of the stored posture; and requires stillness through each 60-second measurement. It shows green or red, with reasons, time-stamped to join the reading. A 15-degree change moves the cuff about 2.4 cm, about 1.2 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 15 x (0.866 - 0.707) = 2.4 cm; 2.4 x 0.49 = 1.2) [D2-02-F17]. The thresholds are OUR ESTIMATE. What the clip cannot see (legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking, a full bladder, smoking) goes into a 4-question phone checklist.
61	
62	![The reading-quality clip](adaptive-care-pictures/13-reading-quality-clip.png)
63	
64	*The kit-built clip checks rest, stillness and arm position; it does not measure blood pressure.*
65	
66	Cuff size matters too: a regular cuff on a large arm reads high [D2-02-F19]. So the app asks the arm size and refuses arms outside the cuff's range; the Omron HEM-7120 standard cuff fits 22-32 cm [D2-02-F30], and it passed an independent validation (ESH-IP 2010) [D2-02-F28].
67	
68	OUR VIEW: the engine refuses to step a dose on readings that fail the clip, so a posture mistake costs a repeat, not a wrong prescription.
69	
70	### 4.6 Was the medicine taken
71	
72	Raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe (chapter 2.1). So before any step-up the chat asks two questions, as buttons (OUR DESIGN):
73	
74	- "In the last 7 days, how many days did you miss your BP tablet? 0 / 1-2 / 3 or more"
75	- "Do you have tablets left for the next 7 days? yes / no"
76	
77	Adherent means 0 missed days. That cut-off is OUR DESIGN and the clinician can change it, because the sheet says "Check for compliance at each visit before titration of dose or addition of drugs" but gives no number. Any missed day, or no tablets left, sends support instead of a step-up, and a card goes to the clinician for information.
78	
79	### 4.7 Safety built into the design
80	
81	The engine runs its checks in a fixed order and proposes a step only at the end (OUR DESIGN, from the sheet):
82	
83	1. A patient who is referred or waiting for lab results is left alone. A patient aged 30 or under, or with diabetes, a past heart attack or stroke, or kidney disease, is flagged "outside the demo, send to the doctor": the sheet has branches for these that tonight's engine does not handle.
84	2. Readings that failed the quality gate are dropped.
85	3. Safety first. A session at or above 180 or 110 brings a request to repeat after rest; if confirmed, an urgent card goes to the doctor and the patient is told to contact the clinic today, ahead of the 30-day wait. This home action is OUR DESIGN; the sheet's 180/110 line is for clinic entry. A low-pressure rule acts only once a clinician sets its threshold.
86	4. Fewer than 3 valid days: ask for more. Under 30 days on the step: "keep going". Home mean below 135/85: "same medicine", no doctor needed.
87	5. At or above the line: the medicine question (chapter 4.6).
88	6. The guards: referral after the last step; referral when pregnancy, or childbearing age without effective contraception, meets a barred drug (amlodipine steps may go ahead); a lab order before telmisartan 80 mg, and for an abnormal value, referral or, with no specialist reachable, withdrawing telmisartan and adding chlorthalidone.
89	7. Only then: propose the next step, quoting the sheet line.
90	
91	Following the written safety rules of OpenAPS, a do-it-yourself insulin system (chapter 2.3) [D2-03-F46], the engine only chooses written regimens, holds the current step when data is missing and never steps on one reading.
92	
93	OUR VIEW: four things are never dropped: valid home readings, the medicine-taken check, a protocol-true proposal with its reasons and safety branches, and a doctor's approval of every change. A dose worked out outside the protocol file, and a language model in the dose path, are ruled out for good.
94	
95	### 4.8 Same loop, new protocol
96	
97	OUR VIEW: each new protocol is a new market on the same engine, approval screen and safety method.
98	
99	| In order | Home signal | Rule in the notes | Status |
100	|---|---|---|---|
101	| 1. High blood pressure | Cuff | Gujarat's ladder; a Nigerian ladder as a second file (chapter 5.2) | Being built tonight |
102	| 2. Insulin, then the tablet steps for diabetes | Sugar meter | The American Diabetes Association's step rule (chapter 2.3) | On paper only |
103	| 3. Heart failure | Weight, pressure, pulse, lab values | Step up to full doses soon after discharge (chapter 2.1) | Roadmap; needs a diagnostics partner |
104	| 4. Warfarin, then asthma | INR meter; inhaler use | Dosing tables differ between sources (search summary only) [D1-06-F37] | Roadmap |
105	
106	![Same loop, new protocol](adaptive-care-pictures/15-same-loop-new-protocol.png)
107	
108	*Diagram: the engine, the approval screen and the chat stay the same; only the home signal and the protocol file change.*
109	
110	The picture says a "doctor or health worker" approves. That is the later aim: only a registered doctor may prescribe (chapter 4.4), and no Indian rule was found that lets a nurse or health officer change a dose (chapter 2.6). It remains a question for counsel.
111	
112	Full detail: Appendix C (technology for each stage, reading quality, protocols as data) and Appendix G (protocol file, decision steps, screens).
113	
114	Chapter 5 shows the smallest version of this product that can be built and tested honestly in one night, and the steps after it.
