1	## Appendix G. The build pack in detail
2	
3	This appendix is tonight's full build pack and the plan for the two steps after it; it supports chapter 5, and the product described in chapter 4. It merges the software note (D2-01) and the hardware note (D2-02) into one schedule, one test list and one list of honest claims for noon. It is also the home of the protocol file and of the parts list and costs.
4	
5	### G1. The ladder: three rungs
6	
7	OUR DESIGN, all three rungs:
8	
9	| Rung | When | What it is | What it proves | What it cannot prove |
10	|---|---|---|---|---|
11	| 1. Tonight | 23:00 Thu 13 Nov to 12:00 Fri 14 Nov | Engine, three screens, reading route, quality clip, tests, simulation | The code does what the protocol sheet says in every listed branch; readings flow end to end; a person can rule on a card in seconds | Anything about patients |
12	| 2. Two-week test | After the event | One clinic, a few patients already on step 1 or 2, their own doctor rules on every proposal | Patients send valid readings and doctors act on proposals inside normal work | Any change in blood pressure control |
13	| 3. 90-day pilot | After rung 2 and approvals | Several clinics, a comparison group | Whether more enrolled patients are under the home line at 90 days | Heart attacks, strokes, deaths |
14	
15	Rung 1 is set out in G2 to G15, rung 2 in G16 and rung 3 in G17.
16	
17	### G2. What gets built tonight
18	
19	OUR DESIGN, from the two build notes:
20	
21	- **The engine.** One pure Python function, `decide()`, reads a protocol file (YAML, a plain-text data format), the patient's state and the week's readings, and returns a proposal with reasons. No input or output, no clock, no randomness. It never computes a dose; it can only pick a regimen written in the file. No language model in the dose path. Stack: Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLite, pydantic, pytest.
22	- **Three screens.** (1) Patient: Telegram chat, same flow on a web form as fallback: measure prompt, photo or typed entry, adherence buttons, change message. (2) Clinician queue: cards sorted urgent first, with step, 7-day sparkline, mean, adherence answer, quoted protocol line, guards ticked, proposed regimen, and Approve, Edit, Reject; a timer is logged. (3) Results: tests, coverage, simulation chart, live-run counts, approve times, protocol dropdown.
23	- **The reading route.** Every route writes {sys, dia, pulse, time, source, quality_flag}. D2-02's order for tonight: a phone photo of any cuff's screen, read by a vision model and confirmed by the patient; an Omron HEM-7156T over Bluetooth with omblepy, only if one is in hand by about 02:00 [D2-02-F1]; typed entry, always built. Photos are read twice, checked for plausible ranges, and shown back for confirmation. Purpose-trained readers reached 0.9-1.2 mmHg mean systolic error on held-out sets, but about 82% of one Guatemalan field set were poor-quality images and errors clustered in the last digit [D2-02-F4]; general vision models are untested on cuff screens [D2-02-F8].
24	- **The quality clip.** An ESP32 with two MPU6050 motion sensors, on the cuff (0x68) and a wrist strap (0x69), on GPIO21 and GPIO22. It enforces 300 seconds of still rest, checks the forearm is near horizontal (within 20 degrees) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of a calibrated posture, holds stillness through each 60-second reading, and posts a valid flag with reasons. It does not measure blood pressure. It targets arm hanging at the side (+6.5/+4.4 mmHg) and arm on the lap (+3.9/+4.0) against arm on a desk, from a crossover randomised trial of 133 adults in Baltimore [D2-02-F16]. Unsensed errors (legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking) go into a phone checklist.
25	
26	The patient chat, the clinician queue and one proposal card in detail are pictured in chapter 4 (mock-ups with example data).
27	
28	### G3. The protocol as a data file
29	
30	The biology student owns these files. Every number carries the sheet's words; a `null` key means "not in the source", and the engine refuses that branch until a clinician fills it. Shortened excerpt of the Gujarat HEARTS file [D1-06-F14]:
31	
32	```yaml
33	population: {age_gt: 30, text: "Measure blood pressure of all adults over 30 years"}
34	steps:
35	  - n: 1
36	    regimen: [{drug: amlodipine, dose_mg: 5}]
37	    text: "Prescribe Amlodipine 5mg"
38	  - n: 2
39	    regimen: [{drug: amlodipine, dose_mg: 10}]
40	    text: "After 30 days measure BP again. If still high: Increase to Amlodipine 10mg"
41	  - n: 3
42	    regimen: [{drug: amlodipine, dose_mg: 10}, {drug: telmisartan, dose_mg: 40}]
43	    text: "Add Telmisartan 40mg"
44	  - n: 4
45	    regimen: [{drug: amlodipine, dose_mg: 10}, {drug: telmisartan, dose_mg: 80}]
46	    text: "Increase to Telmisartan 80mg**"
47	    requires: [blood_sugar, urea, creatinine, urine_protein]   # max_age_days: null
48	    if_any_abnormal: refer
49	    if_no_specialist: {withdraw: telmisartan, add: {drug: chlorthalidone, dose_mg: 12.5}}
50	    text_lab: "If any value is abnormal refer to a specialist. If the patient cannot consult a specialist, withdraw Telmisartan and add Chlorthalidone."
51	  - n: 5
52	    regimen: [amlodipine 10, telmisartan 80, {drug: chlorthalidone, dose_mg: 12.5}]
53	    text: "Add Chlorthalidone 12.5mg***"
54	    substitutes: [{drug: hydrochlorothiazide, dose_mg: 25, if: chlorthalidone_unavailable}]
55	after_last_step:
56	  action: adherence_then_refer
57	  text: "Check if the patient has been taking medications regularly and correctly. If yes, refer to a specialist."
58	contraindications:
59	  - when: [pregnancy, childbearing_age_without_effective_contraception]
60	    blocked_drugs: [telmisartan, chlorthalidone, ace_inhibitors, arbs, thiazide_or_thiazide_like_diuretics, statins]
61	    allowed_drugs: [amlodipine]           # "Calcium channel blocker (CCB) can be used."
62	    if_uncontrolled_on_intensified_dose: refer
63	    action: block_step_and_refer
64	    text: "DO NOT give Telmisartan or Chlorthalidone."
65	out_of_scope:                             # OUR DESIGN: the sheet has these branches; tonight's engine does not
66	  when: [diabetes, past_heart_attack, past_stroke, chronic_kidney_disease]
67	  action: flag_outside_demo_send_to_doctor
68	safety:
69	  very_high: {sbp_gte: 180, dbp_gte: 110, rule: any, action: repeat_then_urgent_review}
70	  low: {sbp_lt: null, action: urgent_review}   # not in the sheet; the supervising clinician sets it
71	```
72	
73	The rule: **the full files are in the D2-01 note** (Gujarat; Nigeria losartan [D1-06-F15]; the ADA basal-insulin rule from the ADA 2025 figure [D1-06-F16], paper only, never run on a person). Copy from there, not from this excerpt, but add what the claims check found missing from the Gujarat file: the age rule, the wider pregnancy rule, the abnormal-lab branch and the out-of-scope flag shown above [D1-06-F14].
74	
75	The two blanks in the D2-01 note's second file are now filled from the Nigeria sheet: "still high" is 140/90 or above, and the pregnancy rule is "DO NOT GIVE losartan to pregnant women nor to women of childbearing age who are not on effective contraception. If pregnant, refer to obstetric specialist". That sheet covers adults 18 and over and has no lab check and no medicine-taken question [D1-06-F15].
76	
77	The very-high action is OUR DESIGN for home readings; the sheet's 180/110 line is for clinic entry [D1-06-F14].
78	
79	### G4. The decision in plain steps
80	
81	1. If the patient is referred or waiting for lab results, do nothing. If the patient is outside the sheet's population (30 or under on the Gujarat file), or has diabetes, a past heart attack or stroke, or kidney disease, flag "outside the demo, send to the doctor": the sheet has branches for these that tonight's engine does not handle [D1-06-F14].
82	2. Keep only readings that passed the quality gate.
83	3. Safety first. Newest session at or above 180 systolic or 110 diastolic: ask for a repeat after rest; if confirmed, raise an urgent card and tell the patient to contact the clinic today. This beats the 30-day wait. The low-pressure branch fires only once a clinician sets its threshold.
84	4. Fewer than 3 valid days: ask for more readings.
85	5. Fewer than 30 days on the step: "keep going".
86	6. Home mean below 135/85: "same medicine", no doctor needed.
87	7. At or above the line: ask the adherence question. Any missed day, or no tablets left: send support, no step-up, card to the clinician for information.
88	8. On the last step: propose referral.
89	9. Pregnant, or a woman of childbearing age not on effective contraception, and the next step has a barred drug (telmisartan, chlorthalidone, or any ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide-type diuretic or statin): propose referral. Amlodipine steps may go ahead; uncontrolled on the intensified amlodipine dose: propose referral [D1-06-F14]. Labs missing before telmisartan 80: propose a lab order. Any lab value abnormal: propose referral, or, if no specialist can be reached, propose withdrawing telmisartan and adding chlorthalidone [D1-06-F14].
90	10. Otherwise propose the next step, quoting the sheet line. Nothing that changes treatment reaches the patient before a clinician approves.
91	
92	The adherence question is two chat buttons: "In the last 7 days, how many days did you miss your BP tablet? 0 / 1-2 / 3 or more" and "Do you have tablets left for the next 7 days? yes / no". Adherent means 0 missed days. That cut-off is OUR DESIGN and the clinician can change it, because the sheet says "Check for compliance at each visit before titration of dose or addition of drugs" but gives no number [D1-06-F14].
93	
94	### G5. The home-reading rule
95	
96	- **Block:** on days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle, two readings 1 minute apart after 5 minutes seated rest, morning before tablets and evening [D2-01-F1, D2-02-F10].
97	- **Valid session:** both readings pass the quality flags; its value is their mean.
98	- **Enough:** at least 3 distinct valid days, aiming for 7. ESH (the European Society of Hypertension) says "Seven-day monitoring (not fewer than 3 days)" [D2-01-F1].
99	- **Day 1:** dropped only if 4 or more valid days remain. ESH calls dropping it a "matter of debate" [D2-02-F12]; the AHA notes some guidelines drop it [D2-02-F10].
100	- **Still high (the home threshold):** mean systolic at or above 135 OR mean diastolic at or above 85. ESH says home 135/85 corresponds to office 140/90 [D2-01-F1]; ISH says home hypertension is readings "consistently 135/85 mm Hg or greater" [D2-01-F3]; the Indian Guidelines IV give above 135/85 (search summary only) [D2-01-F4, D2-02-F15].
101	- **Very high:** any single session at or above 180 or 110.
102	- **Clinic reading in the cycle:** the card shows both; the clinician decides.
103	
104	The Gujarat sheet is written for clinic readings ("SBP 140 or DBP 90") [D1-06-F14]. **Mapping a clinic protocol to home readings at 135/85 is OUR DESIGN.** Say so aloud on the slide, and keep the threshold a protocol value the clinician signs. No Indian home-against-clinic offset was searched.

107	
108	Thirty-six tests, one per branch; exact inputs are in D2-01 section 3c. The rows marked "to add" cover the rules the claims check found on the sheets [D1-06-F14, D1-06-F15]; they have no test numbers or inputs in D2-01 yet.

114	| 30-day interval | T6 | 150/95 after 20 days: keep going | 1 |

116	| Step-ups and guards | T8-T13 | Steps 2 to 5; lab order before telmisartan 80; hydrochlorothiazide substitute | 6 |
117	| Last step | T14 | Referral with the sheet text | 1 |
118	| Pregnancy | T16, T17 | Telmisartan step blocked and referred; amlodipine step allowed | 2 |
119	| Very high and order of checks | T18-T21 | Repeat asked; confirmed gives urgent; diastolic alone counts; safety beats the interval | 4 |
120	| Paused and unset values | T23, T26 | Referred patient untouched; unset low threshold logs a warning | 2 |
121	| Clinic entry rules | T27-T29 | 182/96, 165/95, 145/92 route correctly | 3 |
122	| Second protocol (Nigeria) | T30-T33 | Losartan step with no adherence question; referral; entry at step 2; refuses a file with a null value | 4 |

132	
133	### G7. Hour by hour, 23:00 Thu to 12:00 Fri
134	
135	Roles: **E** engine (CS), **I** interfaces (CS), **P** protocol and tests (biology), **H1** clip, **H2** cuff and photo route (hardware), **L** lead, story and simulation. OUR DESIGN, merged from the two notes; where they clash, this table picks one and the clash is listed below it.

1	## 5. The MVP
2	
3	Chapter 4 showed the whole product. This chapter shows the MVP (minimum viable product: the smallest product that tests the business): what can be built and tested between 23:00 on 13 November and noon on 14 November, what it can honestly prove, and the two rungs after it.
4	
5	### 5.1 The ladder
6	
7	OUR DESIGN, all three rungs:
8	
9	| Rung | When | What it is | What it proves | What it cannot prove |
10	|---|---|---|---|---|
11	| 1. Tonight | To noon, 14 Nov | Engine, three screens, reading route, quality clip, tests, simulation | The code does what the sheet says in every listed branch; readings flow end to end; a person can rule on a card in seconds | Anything about patients |
12	| 2. Two-week test | After the event | One clinic, a few patients on step 1 or 2, their own doctor rules on every proposal | Patients send valid readings and doctors act on proposals inside normal work | Any change in blood pressure control |
13	| 3. 90-day pilot | After rung 2 and approvals | Several clinics, a comparison group | Whether more enrolled patients are under the home line at 90 days | Heart attacks, strokes, deaths |
14	
15	OUR VIEW: each rung earns the next. Going to rung 3 without rung 2 would put an untried loop in front of an ethics committee.

17	### 5.2 Rung 1: what gets built tonight
18	
19	OUR DESIGN, from the two build notes:
20	
21	- **Software.** The `decide()` engine (chapter 4.2), in Python 3.11 with FastAPI, SQLite, pydantic and pytest. Three screens: patient chat, clinician queue, and a results page with a protocol dropdown.
22	- **Hardware.** The photo route and typed entry (chapter 4.3); Bluetooth only if an Omron HEM-7156T is in hand by about 02:00; the quality clip (chapter 4.5); a pill-box sensor as a stretch goal. One non-Bluetooth cuff and small parts cost about ₹2,000-2,600 (OUR ARITHMETIC); night delivery to Sonipat was not confirmed.
23	- **Protocol files**, owned by the biology student: Gujarat; Nigeria's losartan ladder, which covers adults 18 and over and has no lab check and no medicine-taken question [D1-06-F15]; and the American Diabetes Association's basal-insulin rule, on paper only, never run on a person. Four rules the claims check found missing from the first Gujarat file (age, the wider pregnancy rule, abnormal labs, out of scope) are now added.
24	- **Tests.** Thirty-six, one per listed branch, across both protocols and the insulin file; tests for the four added Gujarat rules and the Nigeria rules are still to write. Coverage: every key read by a test, plus line and branch coverage.
25	- **Checkpoints** (the six roles are in Appendix G). 02:00: a typed reading flows to a proposal, an approval and a message. 05:00: engine frozen. 09:30: testing stops. 10:30: backup video recorded.
26	- **Cut lines.** If behind, drop in order: WhatsApp; a third language; 20-seed simulation bands; the insulin file as tests; Nigeria as a live dropdown (keep its tests); Telegram (use the web form); the photo or Bluetooth route (use typed readings). Missing 02:00 drops the first four at once. **Never cut:** the adherence check, clinician approval, the pregnancy and childbearing-age, abnormal-lab, "outside the demo" and very-high branches, the test table and the safety statement.
27	
28	The hardware test uses 6 to 10 volunteer teammates, about 25 minutes each (OUR ESTIMATE), recorded by ID only; anyone at or above 180/110 is told to see a doctor and not tested further. Each is measured in correct posture, arm hanging and arm on the lap, reported as counts and ranges, not p-values. It tests the pipeline and the clip, not cuff accuracy or patients.
29	
30	OUR VIEW: the critical path is the schema, `decide()`, the core tests, the queue with Approve, and the change message. Hardware hangs off it with a typed fallback, so a hardware failure costs a result, not the demo.

57	
58	**The simulated cohort** (OUR SIMULATION, not a trial, no effect on patients) follows 5,000 patients per arm for 12 monthly cycles. Each patient's hidden "responder step" comes from the programme's Punjab control-by-step figures (chapter 2.2); 48% are non-adherent (search summary only; definition-dependent) [D1-03-F44], used only to count needless step-ups. The clinic arm attends each month at the return rate of chapter 1, an ASSUMPTION that favours it; the loop arm sends a valid block in 30%, 50% or 70% of months (ASSUMPTION). First run (seed 1; to be re-run tonight, not quoted as data): control at month 12 was 39.0% in the clinic-only arm and 49.1%, 55.0% and 59.8% in the loop arm at those three levels (OUR SIMULATION).

Both follow from the assumptions. The clinic arm sits between district control and control among returners (chapter 1): plausible, not a validation. OUR VIEW: say this aloud; "the gain comes from contact" is more credible than a dosing claim.

80	
81	For the first slide and the README, word for word:
82	
83	> This is a student prototype built overnight. It is not medical advice and not a medical device. It does not diagnose or treat anyone. A clinician must approve every change of medicine; the software only drafts proposals from a published protocol. No patient data were used tonight. The readings shown are from teammates who volunteered and from synthetic patients; they are not clinical data. The simulation is our own model with stated assumptions, not a trial. Low-blood-pressure and lab-recency limits are deliberately left unset and must be set by a supervising clinician before any real use.

87	### 5.7 Rung 2: two weeks with a doctor in the loop
88	
89	OUR DESIGN. It asks whether the loop survives normal clinic work, not whether it lowers pressure.
90	
91	- **Setting:** as in the ladder above, inside normal consultations. Written consent names the software, as ICMR's guidance on artificial intelligence expects consent and a human in control [D2-04-F35].
92	- **Measured:** days with valid readings per patient; proposals and how the doctor ruled, with reasons; time to rule; answers to the medicine question; any symptoms reported.
93	- **Must not claim:** any change in pressure or control, safety, or clinical effect. Two weeks is shorter than one 30-day step, so few step-ups will happen.
94	- **Ethics:** a desk test on team members is not a clinical investigation on patients [D2-04-F50]; whether this test needs an ethics committee is a question for the clinic and the university.
95	
96	OUR VIEW: rung 2 answers the first stop question: do doctors rule on proposals in time.

98	### 5.8 Rung 3: a 90-day pilot
99	
100	OUR DESIGN unless cited.
101	
102	**Primary endpoint:** the share of all enrolled patients with a home mean under 135/85 at 90 days, counting silent patients as not controlled. It can move within three 30-day steps, India's programme already reports control, and counting silent patients tests the loop where the null Indian trial, mWellcare, did not look: between visits, among those who do not return (chapter 2.1).
103	
104	**Secondary measures:** valid blocks a month; steps taken; time to approve; adverse events, including dizziness, falls and low readings.
105	
106	| Comparison design | Can show | Cannot show |
107	|---|---|---|
108	| Before and after | Change against the clinics' own past | Whether it would have happened anyway |
109	| Matched clinics | A difference against similar clinics at the same time | Freedom from hidden differences |
110	| Staggered start (clinics switch on in random order, as in SMARThealth India [D2-01-F16]) | A fairer comparison, each clinic its own control | Quick results: it needs more clinics and time |
111	
112	**Size** (OUR ARITHMETIC): to tell 40% from 55% controlled (ASSUMPTION) at 5% two-sided significance and 80% power, with 20% drop-out (ASSUMPTION), needs 217 patients per arm, 434 in all, if patients are randomised one by one; randomising by clinic would need more, not computed here. # SPARK Night 2026: the adaptive care challenge, told as one story

**What this is.** The working document for the Beyond Next Ventures challenge at SPARK Night (13-14 Nov 2026, Ashoka University), rewritten on 14 November so that it reads in one line from start to finish. It is the same research as the 13 November edition, in a new order. No fact was changed. Repeated passages were removed, and each topic now sits in one place. One thing is new: a biology deep dive researched on 14 November, marked "new research" wherever it appears (chapter 2.7, one section of chapter 4, and Appendix I). Internal to the team.

**Status.** The research was completed on 13 Nov 2026 at about 11:10 PM. Three claims checks re-opened the sources of about 183 load-bearing facts, and their corrections are applied throughout. Chapter 7 says what was not checked and what was not found.

**The challenge, as set by the fund.**

> We need ways to manage chronic disease burden at scale despite limited access to resources, specialists and irregular clinical follow-ups. Patients need treatment methods that responds to their specific condition, and will remain adaptive to patient needs between appointments. How can digital therapeutics use rapid feedback from medical devices or biomarkers to continuously personalise care, thereby bringing measurable improvements in health outcomes to patients who cannot access frequent specialist support? The opportunity is to extend effective treatment into everyday life, beyond monitoring and reminders.

### How the document is laid out

The story comes first, in the order the argument builds. The answer comes at the end of the story, not at the start. The appendix holds the full detail behind each chapter, each topic in one place.

| Chapter | The question it answers | Full detail in |
|---|---|---|
| 1. The problem | What is the fund asking, who is it about, why does care break down between visits, and why has the market not fixed it | Appendix A |
| 2. What the research found | What actually improves outcomes, how care has been scaled without specialists, what the technology can do, who else is doing this, where the money is, what the rules say, and the biology underneath (new research) | Appendices B, C, D, E and I |
| 3. Analysis: what it all means | Where to play, how to win, which of the options to build and why | Appendix F |
| 4. The product we can build | What the home blood-pressure step loop is and how it works for the patient and the doctor | Appendix G |
| 5. The MVP | What gets built tonight, what can honestly be shown at noon, and what comes after | Appendix G |
| 6. Recommendation, risks and open questions | What to do, how to pitch it, its weak spots, and what the team still has to decide (the old part L) | Appendix H |
| 7. Method and limits | How this was made and how far to trust it (the old part M) | Appendix J (the claim register) |

### Which part to read

| If you are | Read |
|---|---|
| Anyone on the team, first time | Chapters 1 to 6, in order |
| Building the engine and screens | Chapters 4 and 5, then Appendix G, then Appendix C |
| Building the hardware | Chapter 5, then Appendix G (parts and the hardware test), then Appendix C (sensing and reading quality) |
| The biology student | Chapters 2.1, 2.2 and 2.7, then Appendix I (the biology deep dive), then Appendix B, then Appendix G (the protocol file and the test cases) |
| Leading the pitch | Chapters 1 to 6, then Appendix H (the mentor) and Appendix F (strategy and options) |
| Writing the one-page thesis | Appendix G (the draft), chapter 1 (the argument), Appendix A (the numbers) |
| Asked "who else is doing this" | Chapter 2.4, then Appendix D |
| Asked "how big is it" or "is it legal" | Chapters 2.5 and 2.6, then Appendix E |

### How to trust a number here

- **Every fact carries an ID that links to its source**, for example D1-01-F02. Appendix J is the register: what each research note recorded, the link, whether the page was opened or only seen in a search summary, and the verdict of the claims check where one was run. Numbers were read at source by one research agent; the load-bearing ones were then re-checked by a second.
- **"Search summary only"** marks a fact seen only in a search result, not on the page itself.
- **Some statements are ours, and marked so:** OUR VIEW (a judgement), OUR ARITHMETIC or OUR ESTIMATE (a sum or a guess from stated inputs), ASSUMPTION (an input we chose), OUR DESIGN (a design choice of ours), THEIR CLAIM (a company about itself), EXAMPLE (mock-up data). The option scores, the market model, the simulation and the price are all ours.
- **Mock-up screens show example data.** Every name and reading in them is invented.
- **What was not done:** no customer interviews; no measured split of public and private treatment; no current specialist counts; no Indian trial of home readings driving dose steps was found. Each appendix ends with what it could not find.
- **It is not medical or legal advice.** The legal sections say what the texts say and list the questions for a lawyer.

**Contents**

18

20	
21	- **Software.** The `decide()` engine (chapter 4.2), in Python 3.11 with FastAPI, SQLite, pydantic and pytest. Three screens: patient chat, clinician queue, and a results page with a protocol dropdown.
22	- **Hardware.** The photo route and typed entry (chapter 4.3); Bluetooth only if an Omron HEM-7156T is in hand by about 02:00; the quality clip (chapter 4.5); a pill-box sensor as a stretch goal. 23	- **Protocol files**, owned by the biology student: Gujarat; Nigeria's losartan ladder, which covers adults 18 and over and has no lab check and no medicine-taken question [D1-06-F15]; and the American Diabetes Association's basal-insulin rule, on paper only, never run on a person. Four rules the claims check found missing from the first Gujarat file (age, the wider pregnancy rule, abnormal labs, out of scope) are now added.
24	- **Tests.** Thirty-six, one per listed branch, across both protocols and the insulin file; tests for the four added Gujarat rules and the Nigeria rules are still to write. Coverage: every key read by a test, plus line and branch coverage.
25	- **Checkpoints** (the six roles are in Appendix G). 02:00: a typed reading flows to a proposal, an approval and a message. 05:00: engine frozen. 09:30: testing stops. 10:30: backup video recorded.
26	- **Cut lines.** If behind, drop in order: WhatsApp; a third language; 20-seed simulation bands; the insulin file as tests; Nigeria as a live dropdown (keep its tests); Telegram (use the web form); the photo or Bluetooth route (use typed readings). Numbers were read at source by one research agent; the load-bearing ones were then re-checked by a second.
- **"Search summary only"** marks a fact seen only in a search result, not on the page itself.
- **Some statements are ours, and marked so:** OUR VIEW (a judgement), OUR ARITHMETIC or OUR ESTIMATE (a sum or a guess from stated inputs), ASSUMPTION (an input we chose), OUR DESIGN (a design choice of ours), THEIR CLAIM (a company about itself), EXAMPLE (mock-up data). The option scores, the market model, the simulation and the price are all ours.
- **Mock-up screens show example data.** Every name and reading in them is invented.
- **What was not done:** no customer interviews; no measured split of public and private treatment; no current specialist counts; no Indian trial of home readings driving dose steps was found. Each appendix ends with what it could not find.
- **It is not medical or legal advice.** The legal sections say what the texts say and list the questions for a lawyer.

"""Checks on the joined report. Run after join_parts.py and link_facts.py.

Usage:  python check_report.py <report.md> [--links]

Reports
- banned words, em dashes, exclamation marks
- picture links that point to a missing file
- paragraphs and table rows that contain a number but no fact link and no tag
  (OUR ARITHMETIC, OUR ESTIMATE, OUR VIEW, ASSUMPTION, EXAMPLE, THEIR CLAIM, NOT RESEARCHED...)
- with --links: every distinct source URL is requested once and failures are listed
"""
import re
import sys
import urllib.request
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

if hasattr(sys.stdout, "reconfigure"):
    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")

BANNED = [
    "synergy", "revolutionary", "game-changing", "ai-powered", "seamless", "leverage", "utilise", "utilize",
    "robust", "cutting-edge", "innovative", "streamline", "optimise", "optimize", "empower", "unlock",
    "world-class", "best-in-class", "next-gen", "ecosystem", "holistic", "delve", "landscape",
]
TAGS = ("OUR ARITHMETIC", "OUR ESTIMATE", "OUR VIEW", "ASSUMPTION", "EXAMPLE", "THEIR CLAIM", "NOT RESEARCHED",
        "NOT FOUND", "OUR DESIGN", "OUR SIMULATION", "Mock-up", "TARGET")
FACT_LINK = re.compile(r"\[D\d-\d\d-F\d+\]\(|D\d-\d\d-F\d+")
NUMBER = re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z#/-])\d[\d,.]*\s?(%|mmHg|crore|lakh|million|billion|patients|people|points)|[₹$£€]\s?\d")


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        raise SystemExit(__doc__)
    report = Path(sys.argv[1])
    text = report.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    lines = text.splitlines()
    problems = 0

    print("== words and marks")
    for i, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
        if line.startswith(">") or "THEIR CLAIM" in line:
            continue
        low = re.sub(r"\]\([^)]*\)", "]", line.lower())
        low = re.sub(r"\"[^\"]*\"", "", low)
        for w in BANNED:
            if re.search(r"(?<![a-z-])" + re.escape(w) + r"(?![a-z])", low):
                print("  line %d: banned word '%s'" % (i, w))
                problems += 1
        if "—" in line:
            print("  line %d: em dash" % i)
            problems += 1
        if re.search(r"[a-z]!(\s|$)", line) and not line.lstrip().startswith("!["):
            print("  line %d: exclamation mark" % i)
            problems += 1

    print("== pictures")
    for m in re.finditer(r"!\[[^\]]*\]\(([^)]+)\)", text):
        p = report.parent / m.group(1)
        if not p.exists():
            print("  missing picture: " + m.group(1))
            problems += 1

    print("== numbers without a source or a tag")
    untagged, in_code, section = 0, False, ""
    for i, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
        if line.startswith("```"):
            in_code = not in_code
        if in_code:
            continue
        if line.startswith("#"):
            section = line.strip("# ").strip()
            continue
        if line.startswith("|---") or line.startswith("![") or not line.strip():
            continue
        if NUMBER.search(line) and not FACT_LINK.search(line) and not any(t in line for t in TAGS):
            untagged += 1
            if untagged <= 60:
                print("  line %d [%s]: %s" % (i, section[:28], line.strip()[:120]))
    print("  total lines with a number and no source or tag: %d" % untagged)

    if "--links" in sys.argv:
        print("== links")
        urls = sorted(set(u.rstrip(".,") for u in re.findall(r"\]\((https?://[^)\s]+)\)", text)))

        def probe(u):
            try:
                req = urllib.request.Request(u, headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (link check)"}, method="GET")
                with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
                    return u, r.status
            except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
                code = getattr(e, "code", None)
                return u, code if code else type(e).__name__

        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=12) as ex:

"""Check that a restructured edition kept the facts of the original parts.

Usage:  python check_restructure.py <old_parts_dir> <new_parts_dir>

Reports
- fact IDs cited in the old parts but missing from the new parts, and IDs that are new
  (D4 IDs are a later research round and are counted, not flagged; files named *biology* and
  "### ... new research" sections are skipped by the numbers check)
- numbers in the new text that appear nowhere in the old text (to check by hand)
- old-style cross-references left in the new text ("part F2", "tab H", "Decision brief")
- pictures: each should be placed exactly once
- story repetition: how often the most-repeated old facts are cited in the story chapters
- word counts per new part
"""
import collections
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

if hasattr(sys.stdout, "reconfigure"):
    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")

FULL = re.compile(r"D(\d)-(\d\d)-F0*(\d+)")
SHORT = re.compile(r"(D\d-\d\d)-F0*\d+((?:\s*(?:,|and|to)\s*F0*\d+)+)")
URL = re.compile(r"https?://\S+")
PIC = re.compile(r"!\[[^\]]*\]\(([^)]+)\)")
NUM = re.compile(r"(?<![\w.-])\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d+)?")
STALE = re.compile(r"\b[Pp]arts? [A-M](?:\d|\b)|\b[Tt]ab [A-M]\b|\bDecision brief\b|\bsee [A-M]\d\b|\b(?:B|C|D|E|F|G)\d{1,2}\b(?! *\.)")
STORY = ("10", "20", "30", "40", "50", "60")


def ids(text):
    out = collections.Counter()
    for m in FULL.finditer(text):
        out["D%s-%s-F%d" % (m.group(1), m.group(2), int(m.group(3)))] += 1
    for m in SHORT.finditer(text):
        for n in re.findall(r"F0*(\d+)", m.group(2)):
            out["%s-F%d" % (m.group(1), int(n))] += 1
    return out


def numbers(text):
    text = URL.sub(" ", text)
    text = PIC.sub(" ", text)
    text = FULL.sub(" ", text)
    text = re.sub(r"\bF0*\d+\b", " ", text)
    return set(m.group(0).rstrip(",.") for m in NUM.finditer(text))


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        raise SystemExit(__doc__)
    old_dir, new_dir = Path(sys.argv[1]), Path(sys.argv[2])
    old_parts = {p.name: p.read_text(encoding="utf-8") for p in sorted(old_dir.glob("*.md"))}
    new_parts = {p.name: p.read_text(encoding="utf-8") for p in sorted(new_dir.glob("*.md"))}
    old_all, new_all = "\n".join(old_parts.values()), "\n".join(new_parts.values())
    problems = 0

    old_ids, new_ids = set(ids(old_all)), set(ids(new_all))
    print("== fact IDs: %d in old, %d in new" % (len(old_ids), len(new_ids)))
    new_round = sorted(i for i in new_ids - old_ids if i.startswith("D4-"))
    print("  new research (D4) IDs cited: %d" % len(new_round))
    missing, extra = sorted(old_ids - new_ids), sorted(i for i in new_ids - old_ids if not i.startswith("D4-"))
    for label, group in (("missing from new", missing), ("new, not in old", extra)):
        if group:
            problems += len(group)
            print("  %s (%d): %s" % (label, len(group), ", ".join(group)))

    print("== numbers in the new text that are not in the old text")
    old_nums = numbers(old_all)
    unknown = 0
    for name, text in new_parts.items():
        if "biology" in name:
            continue
        new_section = False
        for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1):
            if line.startswith("### "):
                new_section = "new research" in line.lower()
            if new_section or line.startswith("#") or "<!--" in line:
                continue

"""Join the part files in report-parts/dtx into the one adaptive-care document.

Usage:
    python join_parts.py [parts_dir] [out_file]

Parts are joined in file-name order with one blank line between them.
A line that reads exactly <!-- CONTENTS --> is replaced by a contents list
built from the level-2 headings (## ...) of all parts.
"""
import pathlib
import re
import sys

ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
DEFAULT_PARTS = ROOT / "report-parts" / "dtx"
DEFAULT_OUT = ROOT / "SPARK Night 2026 - adaptive care challenge.md"


def slug(heading: str) -> str:
    """GitHub-style anchor for a heading."""
    s = heading.strip().lower()
    s = re.sub(r"[^\w\s-]", "", s, flags=re.UNICODE)
    return re.sub(r"\s+", "-", s)


def main() -> None:
    if hasattr(sys.stdout, "reconfigure"):
        sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
    parts_dir = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else DEFAULT_PARTS
    out = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else DEFAULT_OUT
    parts = sorted(parts_dir.glob("*.md"))
    if not parts:
        sys.exit(f"No part files found in {parts_dir}")

    texts = [p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip() for p in parts]
    doc = "\n\n".join(texts) + "\n"

    in_code = False
    headings = []
    for line in doc.splitlines():
        if line.startswith("```"):
            in_code = not in_code
        elif not in_code and line.startswith("## "):
            headings.append(line[3:].strip())
    contents = "\n".join(f"- [{h}](#{slug(h)})" for h in headings)
    doc = doc.replace("<!-- CONTENTS -->", contents)

    out.write_text(doc, encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")
    words = len(re.findall(r"\S+", doc))
    print(f"Joined {len(parts)} parts -> {out}")
    print(f"{words:,} words, {doc.count(chr(10)):,} lines, {len(headings)} sections")
    for p in parts:
        print("  ", p.name)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Each source was re-opened by a second route. Abstracts came from PubMed E-utilities efetch. Full texts came from Europe PMC fullTextXML, NCBI efetch db=pmc or the PMC article page. Labels came from the DailyMed SPL XML service (v2), and the guidelines from the KDIGO 2024 and ICMR NEDL PDFs, the NICE NG136 page and openFDA 510(k).

10	
11	Corrections:
12	1. GRAND (D3-04-F09 CORRECTED; D4-03-F40 CONFIRMED). Both counts are right but measure different things. The study **enrolled 1,920** treated patients at 18 centres in 12 states (7 regions). Only **1,578 with valid clinic and home readings were analysed**, and every percentage is of the 1,578: 55.9% well controlled, 5.1% white-coat uncontrolled, 21.8% masked uncontrolled, 17.2% sustained uncontrolled, 77.7% vs 55.9% controlled. D3-04-F09 attaches these percentages to "1,920 treated patients", which is wrong. Published online 6 Nov 2026 (Hypertens Res). The 1,920 figure is the denominator of the companion knowledge paper (D4-03-F41).
13	2. D4-05-F11 (OUTREACH). 748 people (not 720) were excluded after visit 1, and 720 of them because they were adherent or their status was unconfirmed. This does not change a product rule.
14	
15	Cautions that bear on product rules (the facts are recorded correctly, but these points limit their use):
16	- The "<10 mmHg fall after a drug is added" trigger (D4-05-F14) is Lane et al.'s rule for **ordering a confirmatory drug assay** in patients on 2 drugs. It is not a non-adherence classifier. At protocol step 3 (adding telmisartan 40 to amlodipine 10), the mean observed fall in the label trial was 11.1 mmHg, of which 3.7 beyond staying on amlodipine 10 (D4-01-F50). So many adherent patients will fall less than 10 mmHg, and the rule will flag them often.
17	- The "77% to 85% per added drug" figure (D4-05-F03) comes from an abstract that says "increase in nonadherence" without naming odds or risk; the full text could not be opened. It is per prescribed drug, not per dose step (steps 2 and 4 add no drug). The product line "risk rises about 1.8 times" turns odds into risk, and the Brazil figure is 1.57 (F07).
18	- The KDIGO 2024 recheck rule (D4-05-F27, F28) is quoted exactly. It is a **CKD** guideline practice point and says "depending on the current GFR and serum potassium". A >30% creatinine rise (PP 3.6.4) is not the same size as a >30% eGFR fall (PP 2.1.4).

20	- D4-03-F11/F61: 4.7 and 5.1 mmHg are the mixed model's **residual SD around each person's own fitted monthly trend**. The paper calls this "short-term intra-participant BP variability" and describes it as the SD of "any 1-week set" (HOMEBP) or of a calendar-month set (TASMINH4). It never says "SD of monthly means". The F61 sums hold, but its stated reason ("includes slow real drift") does not: each person's linear drift is already in the model.

Punjab (D4-03-F31): trained nurses with a sphygmomanometer at home or the workplace, 9 am to 2 pm, mean of 2 readings 5 min apart, in a general community sample (hypertension prevalence 10% to 24%), not treated patients. 3	## Summary
4	
5	Checked 45 fact IDs from `D4-04 Why each safety check exists.md`: every fact named in its Digest (including the "Surprises" line) and in "What this suggests for the product", plus every threshold fact a safety rule would rest on. Routes: PubMed E-utilities `efetch` abstracts (a different route from the note's Europe PMC search links), Europe PMC full text XML for two papers, openFDA label JSON and the DailyMed v2 SPL service for the labels (the note used DailyMed drugInfo pages), and the NICE pages and KDIGO, UKKA and Resolve to Save Lives PDFs re-downloaded and read as text (same URLs; no other route exists for these). Opened 14 Nov 2026.
6	
7	Verdicts: CONFIRMED 43, CORRECTED 2, CONTESTED 0, NOT FOUND 0.
8	
9	Corrections and findings that change a product safety rule:
10	
11	1. D4-04-F62 (CORRECTED). The North Indian "45% in the hot season" is not a rate among diuretic users. It is the share of 247 hospitalised hyponatraemia cases (any cause, adult medical-ward inpatients, case-control stage, King George's Medical University hospitals, Lucknow) that fell in April to June; October to March held 46.6% (115 of 247) and July to September 9% (21 of 247). Per month, April to June is still the busiest (OUR ARITHMETIC: 111 / 3 = 37 a month against 115 / 6 = 19 and 21 / 3 = 7), so a weak seasonal signal exists, but diuretic use was not independently associated with low sodium in this study, patients were middle-aged (mean about 50), and the note's "mainly loop diuretics likely" is wrong (thiazides were the commonest class, 45.9%, in the prevalence stage). The "sodium test within the first month of chlorthalidone ... and the hot season" suggestion should rest on F58 and F61 (first 30 days, older age, low weight, low potassium), with season at most a soft flag.
12	2. Creatinine rule scope (F23, F27, no verdict change). The values are right, but the rule as written in the Digest ("30% or more: look for dehydration or NSAIDs, then stop or reduce") is NICE NG203 1.6.21 wording. KDIGO PP 3.2.5 says "continue ... unless serum creatinine rises by more than 30% within 4 weeks" (strictly above 30%, within 4 weeks) and does not itself give the investigate-then-stop step; KDIGO adds that a rise under 30% does not mandate change "as long as" there is no hyperkalaemia or fluid retention. Both NICE NG203 and KDIGO apply to adults with CKD. The only one of the three that applies to every ACE inhibitor or ARB start is UKKA Guideline 2.3 (urea and electrolytes at 1 to 2 weeks and after every dose titration, grade 1A). The rule engine should cite UKKA for the general case and use "30% or more" (NICE) as the conservative cut-off.
13	3. Potassium bands (F34, confirmed). All bands and windows match. Two details for the rule text: the 3-day recheck reads "within 3 days, or as soon as feasible" for mild hyperkalaemia "detected unexpectedly in the community"; and stopping at K+ 6 or more applies to patients "who do not meet the criteria for treatment with patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate", not "unless on a binder". The UKKA guideline (original July 2020, updated October 2023 and July 2026) carries a review date of October 2026, which has passed.
14	4. First-trimester comparison (F31, F32, no verdict change). Both numbers are right but measure different outcomes: Cooper's RR 2.71 is any major malformation against no antihypertensive; Li's OR 1.14 is congenital heart defects against untreated hypertensive mothers. The like-for-like Li figure is any birth defect, first-trimester-only ACE inhibitor against hypertension controls: adjusted OR 0.97 (0.67 to 1.41) (Li 2011 Table 2). Both studies are ACE-inhibitor data, not ARB data.
15	5. Home orthostatic test (F50, no verdict change). Kappa 0.90 is for lying-to-standing tests in 25 people; the product suggestion is sit-then-stand. NICE 1.1.7 says to repeat lying down if a seated start is negative despite symptoms, and F44's trials (seated to standing) were flagged as missing drops.
16	
17	Other precision fixes: F01 label provenance (PD-Rx Pharmaceuticals repackager listing of an Inventia Healthcare product distributed by Ascend, not Alkem). F12's 14.6% in women pools all doses; do not pair it with the 10.8% at 10 mg. F57: both IHCI sheets do mention "close clinical and biochemical monitoring" for ACE inhibitor or ARB use in chronic kidney disease, with no test or interval, so "no recheck" holds for the main pathway.

1	# D4-06 Claims check - biology part 1 (agent: claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-14)
2	
3	## Summary
4	
5	Checked 96 fact IDs: every fact named in the Digest and "What this suggests for the product" sections of D4-01, D4-03 and D4-05, plus D3-04-F09 for the GRAND clash. Each source was re-opened by a second route. Abstracts came from PubMed E-utilities efetch. Full texts came from Europe PMC fullTextXML, NCBI efetch db=pmc or the PMC article page. Labels came from the DailyMed SPL XML service (v2), and the guidelines from the KDIGO 2024 and ICMR NEDL PDFs, the NICE NG136 page and openFDA 510(k).
6	
7	Counts: CONFIRMED 93, CORRECTED 2, CONTESTED 0, NOT FOUND 1.
8	
9	The research notes recorded their sources faithfully. Every number in the six named checks matched the source. All OUR ARITHMETIC sums in D4-03 (F34, F57, F61, F62) and D4-01 (F49, F50, F21) hold when redone.
10	
11	Corrections:
12	1. GRAND (D3-04-F09 CORRECTED; D4-03-F40 CONFIRMED). Both counts are right but measure different things. The study **enrolled 1,920** treated patients at 18 centres in 12 states (7 regions). Only **1,578 with valid clinic and home readings were analysed**, and every percentage is of the 1,578: 55.9% well controlled, 5.1% white-coat uncontrolled, 21.8% masked uncontrolled, 17.2% sustained uncontrolled, 77.7% vs 55.9% controlled. D3-04-F09 attaches these percentages to "1,920 treated patients", which is wrong. Published online 6 Nov 2026 (Hypertens Res). The 1,920 figure is the denominator of the companion knowledge paper (D4-03-F41).
13	2. D4-05-F11 (OUTREACH). 748 people (not 720) were excluded after visit 1, and 720 of them because they were adherent or their status was unconfirmed. This does not change a product rule.
14	
15	Cautions that bear on product rules (the facts are recorded correctly, but these points limit their use):
16	- The "<10 mmHg fall after a drug is added" trigger (D4-05-F14) is Lane et al.'s rule for **ordering a confirmatory drug assay** in patients on 2 drugs. It is not a non-adherence classifier. At protocol step 3 (adding telmisartan 40 to amlodipine 10), the mean observed fall in the label trial was 11.1 mmHg, of which 3.7 beyond staying on amlodipine 10 (D4-01-F50). So many adherent patients will fall less than 10 mmHg, and the rule will flag them often.
17	- The "77% to 85% per added drug" figure (D4-05-F03) comes from an abstract that says "increase in nonadherence" without naming odds or risk; the full text could not be opened. It is per prescribed drug, not per dose step (steps 2 and 4 add no drug). The product line "risk rises about 1.8 times" turns odds into risk, and the Brazil figure is 1.57 (F07).
18	- The KDIGO 2024 recheck rule (D4-05-F27, F28) is quoted exactly. It is a **CKD** guideline practice point and says "depending on the current GFR and serum potassium". A >30% creatinine rise (PP 3.6.4) is not the same size as a >30% eGFR fall (PP 2.1.4).
19	- The noise bands in D4-03-F33/F34 come from **untreated** IDH participants (mean home BP 115/77). Treated older patients vary more (F10), so the 8.5 and 12.5 mmHg change thresholds are probably too narrow for the loop's patients.
20	- D4-03-F11/F61: 4.7 and 5.1 mmHg are the mixed model's **residual SD around each person's own fitted monthly trend**. The paper calls this "short-term intra-participant BP variability" and describes it as the SD of "any 1-week set" (HOMEBP) or of a calendar-month set (TASMINH4). It never says "SD of monthly means". The F61 sums hold, but its stated reason ("includes slow real drift") does not: each person's linear drift is already in the model.
21	- The seasonal figures are not home-cuff data. Punjab (D4-03-F31): trained nurses with a sphygmomanometer at home or the workplace, 9 am to 2 pm, mean of 2 readings 5 min apart, in a general community sample (hypertension prevalence 10% to 24%), not treated patients. Delhi (F32): readings at 4 investigator home visits in normotensive women aged 18 to 40.
22	- D4-01-F03: the "generally much larger" variation sentence is in PHYSIC's Introduction and cites earlier studies; it is not a PHYSIC result. PHYSIC's 4.4 mmHg is model-based ("assuming the fitted model to be true").
23	
24	## Checks
25	
26	| Fact ID | Claim as recorded | Verdict | What was found |
27	|---|---|---|---|

3	## Summary
4	
5	Checked 45 fact IDs from `D4-04 Why each safety check exists.md`: every fact named in its Digest (including the "Surprises" line) and in "What this suggests for the product", plus every threshold fact a safety rule would rest on. Routes: PubMed E-utilities `efetch` abstracts (a different route from the note's Europe PMC search links), Europe PMC full text XML for two papers, openFDA label JSON and the DailyMed v2 SPL service for the labels (the note used DailyMed drugInfo pages), and the NICE pages and KDIGO, UKKA and Resolve to Save Lives PDFs re-downloaded and read as text (same URLs; no other route exists for these). Opened 14 Nov 2026.
6	
7	Verdicts: CONFIRMED 43, CORRECTED 2, CONTESTED 0, NOT FOUND 0.
8	
9	Corrections and findings that change a product safety rule:
10	
11	1. D4-04-F62 (CORRECTED). The North Indian "45% in the hot season" is not a rate among diuretic users. It is the share of 247 hospitalised hyponatraemia cases (any cause, adult medical-ward inpatients, case-control stage, King George's Medical University hospitals, Lucknow) that fell in April to June; October to March held 46.6% (115 of 247) and July to September 9% (21 of 247). Per month, April to June is still the busiest (OUR ARITHMETIC: 111 / 3 = 37 a month against 115 / 6 = 19 and 21 / 3 = 7), so a weak seasonal signal exists, but diuretic use was not independently associated with low sodium in this study, patients were middle-aged (mean about 50), and the note's "mainly loop diuretics likely" is wrong (thiazides were the commonest class, 45.9%, in the prevalence stage). The "sodium test within the first month of chlorthalidone ... and the hot season" suggestion should rest on F58 and F61 (first 30 days, older age, low weight, low potassium), with season at most a soft flag.
12	2. Creatinine rule scope (F23, F27, no verdict change). The values are right, but the rule as written in the Digest ("30% or more: look for dehydration or NSAIDs, then stop or reduce") is NICE NG203 1.6.21 wording. KDIGO PP 3.2.5 says "continue ... unless serum creatinine rises by more than 30% within 4 weeks" (strictly above 30%, within 4 weeks) and does not itself give the investigate-then-stop step; KDIGO adds that a rise under 30% does not mandate change "as long as" there is no hyperkalaemia or fluid retention. Both NICE NG203 and KDIGO apply to adults with CKD. The only one of the three that applies to every ACE inhibitor or ARB start is UKKA Guideline 2.3 (urea and electrolytes at 1 to 2 weeks and after every dose titration, grade 1A). The rule engine should cite UKKA for the general case and use "30% or more" (NICE) as the conservative cut-off.
13	3. Potassium bands (F34, confirmed). All bands and windows match. Two details for the rule text: the 3-day recheck reads "within 3 days, or as soon as feasible" for mild hyperkalaemia "detected unexpectedly in the community"; and stopping at K+ 6 or more applies to patients "who do not meet the criteria for treatment with patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate", not "unless on a binder". The UKKA guideline (original July 2020, updated October 2023 and July 2026) carries a review date of October 2026, which has passed.
14	4. First-trimester comparison (F31, F32, no verdict change). Both numbers are right but measure different outcomes: Cooper's RR 2.71 is any major malformation against no antihypertensive; Li's OR 1.14 is congenital heart defects against untreated hypertensive mothers. The like-for-like Li figure is any birth defect, first-trimester-only ACE inhibitor against hypertension controls: adjusted OR 0.97 (0.67 to 1.41) (Li 2011 Table 2). Both studies are ACE-inhibitor data, not ARB data.
15	5. Home orthostatic test (F50, no verdict change). Kappa 0.90 is for lying-to-standing tests in 25 people; the product suggestion is sit-then-stand. NICE 1.1.7 says to repeat lying down if a seated start is negative despite symptoms, and F44's trials (seated to standing) were flagged as missing drops.
16	
17	Other precision fixes: F01 label provenance (PD-Rx Pharmaceuticals repackager listing of an Inventia Healthcare product distributed by Ascend, not Alkem). F12's 14.6% in women pools all doses; do not pair it with the 10.8% at 10 mg. F57: both IHCI sheets do mention "close clinical and biochemical monitoring" for ACE inhibitor or ARB use in chronic kidney disease, with no test or interval, so "no recheck" holds for the main pathway.

## Appendix I. Biology deep dive (new research, 14 Nov)

This appendix is the biology underneath the step loop, written for the team's biology student, who will turn it into protocol rules. It explains how each protocol drug lowers pressure, who responds to which drug, how fast a step works, how much home readings move on their own, why each safety check exists, which blood and urine tests matter, and how the body can show whether a medicine was taken. Chapter 2.7 tells it in short, and chapter 4.9 lists the product features it suggests.

### I1. How to read this appendix

- **New research.** Five research notes were written in the early hours of 14 Nov 2026, after the rest of this document: who responds to what (D4-01), how fast a dose change works (D4-02), natural variation and how many readings (D4-03), why each safety check exists (D4-04), and biomarkers and adherence signals (D4-05). Their fact IDs start with D4.
- **Claims checks.** Three checks re-opened the sources by a second route: D4-06 (the main facts of D4-01, D4-03 and D4-05), D4-07 (D4-04) and D4-08 (D4-02). Where a check corrected a fact, the text gives the corrected value and says "(corrected in the claims check)". Where a check confirmed a fact but limited how it can be used, the text says "(claims check)". A fact a check could not re-find is left out. Facts the checks did not reach carry no verdict. Appendix J gives the verdict for every ID.
- **What was opened.** Mostly primary sources: US drug labels (full text), guideline texts from NICE, KDIGO (the international kidney guideline group), the UK Kidney Association (UKKA), WHO 2021, ESH 2023 and an ISH 2020 author copy, India's state protocol sheets for Punjab, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra, Nigeria's sheet, India's national list of essential diagnostics (ICMR, 2025), and papers through Europe PMC. Many trials were read as abstracts only, and the text says so where it matters. A few facts were seen only in a search summary and are marked "(search summary only)", including two guideline algorithms and every Indian test price.
- **What was not opened.** The Gujarat sheet was not reopened in this round; the other Indian sheets stand in for it. Indian package inserts, Indian guideline texts and the full US guideline texts were not opened.
- **India data are thin.** No trial in Indian or South Asian patients rotated each person through several drug families. No Indian study measured adherence with a drug assay. No Indian data on how much one person's home readings vary were found, and Indian seasonal data come from readings taken by nurses or investigators, not home cuffs. Most numbers below come from the US, the UK, the Nordic countries and Japan, and each says where it was measured.
- **Tags.** As in the rest of the document: OUR VIEW (a judgement), OUR ARITHMETIC (a sum, shown), OUR DESIGN (a design choice of ours), "(search summary only)".
- **Not medical advice.** This appendix is not medical advice. Medicines and doses appear only as written in a label, guideline, protocol sheet or trial. Every change it suggests (I9, I10) is a question for the team and a supervising clinician, and the state protocol stays as written.

### I2. How the protocol's drugs lower pressure

The Gujarat ladder uses three families of drug, and each pulls a different lever: the muscle in the walls of the small arteries, the angiotensin hormone system that tightens those arteries, and the kidney's handling of salt. Knowing the lever explains who responds, how fast, and which side effects and lab changes to expect.

#### Amlodipine: relaxes the small arteries

Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker. It "inhibits the transmembrane influx of calcium ions" into the smooth muscle of blood vessels more than into heart muscle, so the arterioles (the smallest arteries) relax and peripheral resistance falls [D4-01-F17]. It attaches to and leaves its binding site slowly, "resulting in a gradual onset of effect", and on daily dosing it causes no significant change in heart rate or in catecholamines (adrenaline-type stress hormones) [D4-01-F17]. In people with high blood pressure it also lowers resistance in the kidney's vessels and raises GFR (glomerular filtration rate: how much blood the kidneys filter each minute) [D4-01-F17]. Its half-life (the time for the blood level to fall by half) is about 30 to 50 hours [D4-02-F01].

#### Telmisartan and losartan: block angiotensin II

Telmisartan is an ARB (angiotensin II receptor blocker). It blocks angiotensin II at the AT1 receptor, over 3,000-fold more than at the AT2 receptor, in blood-vessel muscle and in the adrenal gland, so it blocks the vessel tightening and the aldosterone release that angiotensin II drives [D4-01-F20]. Aldosterone drives the kidney's collecting duct to pass potassium, which is why the potassium rules in I6 exist [D4-04-F06]. Angiotensin II normally holds renin down; once it is blocked, renin and angiotensin II rise in the blood, "but the resulting increased plasma renin activity and angiotensin II circulating levels do not overcome the effect" [D4-01-F20]. At 80 mg telmisartan blocked the pressure rise from infused angiotensin II by about 90% at peak and about 40% at 24 hours [D4-01-F20]. In healthy volunteers it did not change plasma aldosterone at doses up to 80 mg [D4-05-F18]. Its half-life is about 24 hours, and it leaves the body almost entirely in bile, not urine [D4-02-F05].

Losartan, on Nigeria's sheet, blocks the same receptor with an extra step: about 14% of a dose is turned by two liver enzymes (CYP2C9 and CYP3A4) into an active metabolite 10 to 40 times more potent, with a half-life of 6 to 9 hours against 2 hours for losartan itself [D4-01-F25]. Removing angiotensin II's feedback doubles to triples plasma renin activity [D4-01-F25].

In the kidney, angiotensin II also keeps the efferent arteriole tight (the small vessel that leaves each glomerulus, the kidney's filter), and that tone holds up filtration [D4-04-F52]. Blocking it relaxes this vessel, so filtration pressure falls and creatinine rises a little (I6) [D4-04-F26].

#### Chlorthalidone and hydrochlorothiazide: make the kidney pass more salt

Both are thiazide-type diuretics. Chlorthalidone raises sodium and chloride loss in urine; its label places the action in the "cortical diluting segment of the ascending limb of Henle's loop", which modern texts call the distal convoluted tubule [D4-01-F23]. It lowers extracellular and plasma volume and cardiac output, and the label says "sodium and water depletion appear to provide a basis for its antihypertensive effect" [D4-01-F23]. Its diuresis (extra urine) starts about 2.6 hours after a dose and lasts up to 72 hours, and its half-life is about 40 to 60 hours [D4-01-F23]. Hydrochlorothiazide also acts on the distal tubule; by shrinking plasma volume it raises renin, aldosterone and potassium loss in urine, and its label calls the pressure-lowering mechanism "not fully understood" [D4-01-F24]. Its diuresis lasts about 6 to 12 hours and its half-life is 5.6 to 14.8 hours [D4-01-F24, D4-02-F11].

The thiazide effect changes over weeks. In 11 patients on hydrochlorothiazide 50 mg twice daily (a high dose, in a small 1978 Western study), pressure, cardiac output and plasma volume had fallen at 48 hours while peripheral resistance had risen as a reflex; at 6 and 8 weeks resistance had fallen and cardiac output was back to baseline [D4-02-F39]. So the early fall comes from salt and water loss, and the lasting fall from more relaxed vessels. In 23 patients on chlorthalidone 100 mg a day for 6 weeks (well above today's doses), body sodium fell, renin rose markedly and the pressure response to noradrenaline fell [D4-02-F40].

#### Why the families are combined

| Pair | What the first drug provokes | What the second does about it |
|---|---|---|
| Thiazide + ARB | Shrinking plasma volume raises renin and aldosterone | The ARB blocks exactly that counter-response; adding telmisartan to hydrochlorothiazide gave an extra fall "similar in magnitude" to telmisartan alone [D4-01-F22] |
| Amlodipine + ARB | Widening the arterioles is thought to raise pressure inside the capillaries, so fluid leaks into the ankles [D4-04-F65] | Adding an ARB or ACE inhibitor cut ankle swelling by 38% [D4-04-F66]. Why is not stated in the sources checked; the notes' explanation (these drugs also widen the vein side) was not confirmed |
| Any two families | Each acts on a different lever | In 42 factorial trials (10,968 people) the effects simply added up: observed against expected 1.01 [D4-01-F09] |

**For the loop (OUR VIEW).** Steps 3 and 5 add a new lever; steps 2 and 4 push the same lever harder. The mechanisms predict that the new levers do more, and I3 shows that they do.

### I3. Who responds to what

People differ in which drug family lowers their pressure most. This section gives the physiology behind it, the trials that measured it, the traits that predict it, what gene tests can and cannot do, and what each Gujarat step adds in mmHg.

#### Two kinds of high pressure

The Cambridge rotation trial proposed that some people's high pressure is driven mainly by renin and angiotensin, and others' mainly by salt and fluid volume [D4-01-F04]. A renin-angiotensin blocker works when the pressure is renin-driven; a diuretic works when it is volume-driven, which shows as low renin [D4-01-F06]. Calcium blockers act directly on the muscle of the arterioles and work across renin levels [D4-01-F06, D4-01-F13]. A salty diet suppresses renin, so a renin-angiotensin blocker then has less to block [D4-01-F13].

| Study | Who, where, how long | What it found |
|---|---|---|
| VA renin re-analysis [D4-01-F06] | 1,031 US men with renin measured, in a single-drug trial | At diastolic 95-99, hydrochlorothiazide worked in 82%, 78% and 14% of those with low, medium and high renin; captopril (an ACE inhibitor) in 51%, 83% and 100%; diltiazem (a calcium blocker) in 83%, 82% and 83%. Age and race predicted response better than renin (P<.001 against P=.05) |
| PEAR [D4-01-F14] | 363 US patients aged 65 or under (152 Black, 211 white), atenolol and hydrochlorothiazide in either order, home readings | Higher renin predicted more response to atenolol and less to hydrochlorothiazide, independent of race and age |
| Salt trial [D4-01-F13] | 391 salt-sensitive US patients, enalapril (an ACE inhibitor) against isradipine (a calcium blocker), alternating high salt (about 315 mmol sodium a day) and low salt (about 90) | The high-minus-low salt difference was -3.6/-1.6 to -8.1/-5.3 mmHg across groups with isradipine against -9.0/-5.3 to -11.8/-7.0 with enalapril: the calcium blocker lost less effect on high salt. On low salt the two drugs were similar |

#### Rotation and crossover trials

Chapter 2.3 gave PHYSIC's headline. In these trials each person takes several drug families in turn, so the trial can see whether a person's best drug differs from the average.

| Trial | Who, where, how long | What it found |
|---|---|---|
| PHYSIC [D4-01-F01, D4-01-F02, D4-01-F03] | Sweden, one centre, 280 randomised and 270 analysed (mean age 64, mild hypertension). Lisinopril 20 mg, candesartan 16 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg and amlodipine 10 mg in random order, two of them repeated; each period a 1-week placebo washout, 2 weeks of dose increase and at least 4 weeks at full dose; daytime ambulatory (24-hour monitor) readings | Each person's best drug gave 4.4 mmHg lower systolic pressure than a fixed choice, and 3.1 mmHg against lisinopril, the best on average; both are model estimates (claims check). Real differences between people appeared between a renin-angiotensin blocker and amlodipine or the thiazide. Large differences were excluded within those two pairs, which is not the same as none |
| Cambridge rotation [D4-01-F04] | 56 untreated young UK patients (mean 161/98), one month each on an ACE inhibitor (A), a beta-blocker (B), a calcium blocker (C) and a diuretic (D); 36 completed all four; 1999 | Control on one drug rose from 39% on the first drug to 73% on each person's best (p=0.0001). Responses to A and B went together (r=0.5), and to C and D (r=0.6), not across the pairs |
| GENRES [D4-01-F32] | 208 Finnish men aged 35-60; amlodipine 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg and losartan 50 mg for 4 weeks each, with 4-week placebo gaps; 24-hour readings | Median falls 11/8 (bisoprolol), 9/6 (losartan), 7/5 (amlodipine) and 5/2 mmHg (hydrochlorothiazide); the same AB/CD split. Amlodipine and thiazide responses grew with age, with higher pressure on placebo and with less night-time dipping. Men only |

PHYSIC's authors say the gain from choosing per person is about twice that of doubling a first drug's dose and more than half that of adding a second drug [D4-01-F03].

A warning comes from a larger data set. In individual data from 7 placebo-controlled trials of ACE-inhibitor regimens (28,281 people, change at 3 months, clinic readings), only 3% of the apparent spread in systolic response between people was real; the rest was ordinary variation [D4-03-F55]. OUR VIEW: the two findings fit. PHYSIC repeated each drug and used ambulatory readings, so it could see a real but modest difference between families; one patient's single before-and-after change mostly shows noise.

#### Traits that predict response

| Trait | What the trials show | India or South Asia |
|---|---|---|
| Age | Amlodipine's systolic effect is greater in older patients, "perhaps because of greater baseline systolic pressure" [D4-01-F18]. In an open US community trial of amlodipine (1,084 patients, 4 weeks of titration then 12 weeks, no placebo), 91.5% of those 65 or over reached goal against 84.1% under 65 [D4-01-F39]. The telmisartan label says its effect is "not influenced by patient age, gender, weight, or body mass index" [D4-01-F21] | No data found |
| Sex | In the same amlodipine trial 91.4% of women reached goal against 83.0% of men, not explained by weight, dose or compliance [D4-01-F39]. Ankle swelling on amlodipine, all doses pooled, was 14.6% in women against 5.6% in men [D4-01-F19]. Across 51 trials (358,636 people) each 5 mmHg fall cut heart events equally in women and men [D4-01-F38] | No data found |
| Salt | See the salt trial above [D4-01-F13] | North-east India, 374 volunteers, 7 days of low then 7 days of high salt: 47.6% of people with high pressure were salt-sensitive, and an extra-salt habit doubled the odds (OR 1.99) [D4-01-F47]. UK Bangladeshi patients with kidney disease (56, 6 months): low-salt advice lowered 24-hour pressure 8/2 mmHg on top of drugs [D4-01-F48] |
| African ancestry | 35 trials (25,540 people): calcium blockers and diuretics lowered pressure more than ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers [D4-01-F11]. CREOLE (728 Black patients, six sub-Saharan countries, 6 months): pairs containing amlodipine lowered 24-hour systolic pressure about 3 mmHg more than perindopril plus hydrochlorothiazide [D4-01-F12]. Telmisartan's effect is "noticeably less" in Black patients, "usually a low-renin population" [D4-01-F21] | Relevant to the Nigerian sheet |
| South Asian ancestry | ASCOT (UK and Nordic countries, 132 South Asian patients): adding perindopril (an ACE inhibitor) to amlodipine changed systolic pressure by -6.2 mmHg, against -1.7 in white and +0.8 in Black patients (interaction P=0.004) [D4-01-F07] | 16 trials with 1,719 South Asian patients, mostly in India, median 8 weeks, low quality: "no significant difference" between drug families [D4-01-F11] |
| Body weight | 232 obese patients, 12 weeks: lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide both worked [D4-01-F41]; no usable weight rule for the protocol drugs [D4-01-F42] | No data found |

#### What the guidelines do with this

- NICE (UK, 2019) is the only guideline found with an age and ancestry rule: an ACE inhibitor or ARB first for adults with type 2 diabetes, or under 55 and not of Black African or African-Caribbean origin; a calcium blocker first for those 55 or over, or of Black African or African-Caribbean origin, without diabetes [D4-01-F15]. It has no South Asian rule [D4-01-F15]. Its committee wrote: "No evidence for step 2 or step 3 treatment was identified that was relevant to determining the best sequence" [D4-01-F16].
- WHO 2021 lets any of three families start (thiazide-type, ACE inhibitor or ARB, long-acting calcium blocker), with no profile rule (search summary only) [D4-01-F43]. ISH 2020 has a rule for Black patients only (search summary only) [D4-01-F44]. ESH 2023 and the US 2017 guideline have no age-based first-drug rule [D4-01-F54].
- India's IHCI starts amlodipine 5 mg in every state except for chronic kidney disease, where telmisartan comes first, and budget-bound procurement was a stated reason [D4-01-F46]. The state documents say amlodipine needs no metabolic monitoring and can be given to women of childbearing age (search summary only) [D4-01-F46].

#### Gene tests and their limits

- In the Finnish GENRES study (228 men, each on four drugs), only one gene signal reached genome-wide significance, for bisoprolol, and it did not replicate [D4-01-F33]. Polygenic scores (built from 793 to over 1 million variants) did not predict response to any of the four drugs [D4-01-F34].
- The largest single-gene effect found was about 3 mmHg: the YEATS4 C/C genotype gave 3.4/2.5 mmHg more response to hydrochlorothiazide in 746 US patients, and it has not been tested in South Asians [D4-01-F35].
- A 2025 review says clinical use "remains challenging", polygenic scores for treatment remain "premature", each common variant moves systolic pressure by about 1 mmHg, and gene-based dosing advice exists for the beta-blocker metoprolol but not for amlodipine, telmisartan or the thiazides [D4-01-F36]. South Asian gene claims for amlodipine and ACE inhibitors are hypotheses in a teaching case, and ASCOT points the other way [D4-01-F37].

#### Raising a dose against adding a drug

| Analysis | Size | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Law and Wald 2003 [D4-01-F08] | 354 placebo-controlled trials, about 40,000 treated | Half the standard dose gave 20% less fall (7.1/4.4 against 9.1/5.5 mmHg); families added up; side effects of thiazides, beta-blockers and calcium blockers rose steeply with dose, while ARBs caused no excess symptoms |
| Wald 2009 [D4-01-F09] | 42 factorial trials, 10,968 people | Adding a second family roughly doubled the fall; doubling one drug's dose gave about one fifth (0.22) of that extra |
| Wang 2025 [D4-01-F10] | 484 placebo-controlled trials, 104,176 people, mean 8.6 weeks | A standard-dose single drug lowered systolic pressure 8.7 mmHg; each dose doubling added 1.5; a two-drug combination gave 14.9 |
| ARBs, Cochrane [D4-01-F52] | 46 trials, 13,451 people | Half the maximum dose gives 80% of the maximum fall; no ARB beat another |
| Thiazides, Cochrane [D4-01-F26] | 60 trials, 11,282 people, mean 8 weeks | Hydrochlorothiazide is dose-related (12.5 mg 6/3, 25 mg 8/3, 50 mg 11/5 mmHg); chlorthalidone 12.5-75 mg gave 12/4 mmHg with no dose dependence (low-quality evidence) |
| Quarter doses [D4-01-F27] | 42 trials, 20,284 people | Two drugs at a quarter dose each matched one drug at standard dose, with side effects no different from placebo |

The low-dose triple pill has been tested in South Asia. In TRIUMPH (Sri Lanka, 11 hospital clinics, 700 patients, 6 months, open-label, against usual care), one pill of telmisartan 20 mg, amlodipine 2.5 mg and chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (the protocol's three drugs at low dose) brought 70% to target against 55%, with dizziness, near-fainting or fainting in 5.2% against 2.8% [D4-01-F28]. GMRx2 (1,385 people in seven countries including Sri Lanka, double-blind, 12 weeks, funded by George Medicines) found a triple pill lowered home systolic pressure 2.5-5.4 mmHg more than each two-drug pair [D4-01-F29].

#### What each Gujarat step adds

The closest source is the US label of the telmisartan-amlodipine combination, whose trials use the Gujarat drugs and doses (8 weeks each; place not stated in the label).

| Gujarat step | Extra systolic fall | Cost of the step |
|---|---|---|
| 2. Amlodipine 5 to 10 mg | 5.3 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 18.2 - 12.9, placebo-subtracted, 1,461 patients) [D4-01-F49] | Ankle swelling 3.0% at 5 mg against 10.8% at 10 mg [D4-01-F19] |
| 3. Add telmisartan 40 mg | 4.0 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 22.2 - 18.2) [D4-01-F49]; 3.7 mmHg beyond staying on amlodipine 10 mg, in 947 patients not controlled on it [D4-01-F50] | Kidney and potassium checks (I6) |
| 4. Telmisartan 40 to 80 mg | 1.7 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 23.9 - 22.2) [D4-01-F49]; 0.2 mmHg in the 947 patients above (OUR ARITHMETIC: 11.3 - 11.1, a cross-arm difference not formally tested) [D4-01-F50]; -1 to +4 mmHg from the telmisartan label's ranges (OUR ARITHMETIC, as redone in the claims check) [D4-01-F21] | Four lab tests on the Gujarat sheet |
| 5. Add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg | About 6.2 mmHg when hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg was added to amlodipine 10 mg plus valsartan (another ARB), in 2,271 patients starting at 170/107, with no placebo arm [D4-01-F53] | Potassium, sodium, uric acid and sugar (I6) |

One more trial bears on step 2. In 1,097 patients not controlled on amlodipine 5 mg, adding telmisartan 40 mg lowered pressure 2.4/1.4 mmHg more than raising amlodipine to 10 mg, with ankle swelling in 4.3% against 27.2% [D4-01-F51]. And chlorthalidone 12.5 mg already sits near the top of its dose curve [D4-01-F26].

India's programme shows similar steps in practice. In Punjab, where step 2 raises amlodipine, clinic control among patients still in care went from 70% to 75%; in Maharashtra, where step 2 adds telmisartan 40 mg, from 76% to 81% [D4-01-F45]. These are control levels at the latest visit after a median 12 months of treatment, among patients who returned, not the effect of one 30-day step (claims check) [D4-02-F17].

**For the loop (OUR VIEW).** Adding or switching a drug family is where the millimetres are. Raising a dose buys little, and step 4 buys almost nothing while it triggers four lab tests. In South Asian patients no family stands out, so the protocol's fixed order is defensible, and age, sex and salt habit are the cheap traits worth recording. Gene and renin tests are not ready for the loop.
