At 80 mg telmisartan blocked the pressure rise from infused angiotensin II by about 90% at peak and about 40% at 24 hours [D4-01-F20]. In healthy volunteers it did not change plasma aldosterone at doses up to 80 mg [D4-05-F18]. Its half-life is about 24 hours, and it leaves the body almost entirely in bile, not urine [D4-02-F05].

Losartan, on Nigeria's sheet, blocks the same receptor with an extra step: about 14% of a dose is turned by two liver enzymes (CYP2C9 and CYP3A4) into an active metabolite 10 to 40 times more potent, with a half-life of 6 to 9 hours against 2 hours for losartan itself [D4-01-F25]. Removing angiotensin II's feedback doubles to triples plasma renin activity [D4-01-F25].

In the kidney, angiotensin II also keeps the efferent arteriole tight (the small vessel that leaves each glomerulus, the kidney's filter), and that tone holds up filtration [D4-04-F52]. Blocking it relaxes this vessel, so filtration pressure falls and creatinine rises a little (I6) [D4-04-F26].

#### Chlorthalidone and hydrochlorothiazide: make the kidney pass more salt

Both are thiazide-type diuretics. Chlorthalidone raises sodium and chloride loss in urine; its label places the action in the "cortical diluting segment of the ascending limb of Henle's loop", which modern texts call the distal convoluted tubule [D4-01-F23]. It lowers extracellular and plasma volume and cardiac output, and the label says "sodium and water depletion appear to provide a basis for its antihypertensive effect" [D4-01-F23]. Its diuresis (extra urine) starts about 2.6 hours after a dose and lasts up to 72 hours, and its half-life is about 40 to 60 hours [D4-01-F23]. Hydrochlorothiazide also acts on the distal tubule; by shrinking plasma volume it raises renin, aldosterone and potassium loss in urine, and its label calls the pressure-lowering mechanism "not fully understood" [D4-01-F24]. Its diuresis lasts about 6 to 12 hours and its half-life is 5.6 to 14.8 hours [D4-01-F24, D4-02-F11].

The thiazide effect changes over weeks. In 11 patients on hydrochlorothiazide 50 mg twice daily (a high dose, in a small 1978 Western study), pressure, cardiac output and plasma volume had fallen at 48 hours while peripheral resistance had risen as a reflex; at 6 and 8 weeks resistance had fallen and cardiac output was back to baseline [D4-02-F39]. So the early fall comes from salt and water loss, and the lasting fall from more relaxed vessels. In 23 patients on chlorthalidone 100 mg a day for 6 weeks (well above today's doses), body sodium fell, renin rose markedly and the pressure response to noradrenaline fell [D4-02-F40].

#### Why the families are combined

| Pair | What the first drug provokes | What the second does about it |
|---|---|---|
| Thiazide + ARB | Shrinking plasma volume raises renin and aldosterone | The ARB blocks exactly that counter-response; adding telmisartan to hydrochlorothiazide gave an extra fall "similar in magnitude" to telmisartan alone [D4-01-F22] |
| Amlodipine + ARB | Widening the arterioles is thought to raise pressure inside the capillaries, so fluid leaks into the ankles [D4-04-F65] | Adding an ARB or ACE inhibitor cut ankle swelling by 38% [D4-04-F66]. Why is not stated in the sources checked; the notes' explanation (these drugs also widen the vein side) was not confirmed |
| Any two families | Each acts on a different lever | In 42 factorial trials (10,968 people) the effects simply added up: observed against expected 1.01 [D4-01-F09] |

**For the loop (OUR VIEW).** Steps 3 and 5 add a new lever; steps 2 and 4 push the same lever harder. The mechanisms predict that the new levers do more, and I3 shows that they do.

### I3. Who responds to what

People differ in which drug family lowers their pressure most. This section gives the physiology behind it, the trials that measured it, the traits that predict it, what gene tests can and cannot do, and what each Gujarat step adds in mmHg.

#### Two kinds of high pressure

The Cambridge rotation trial proposed that some people's high pressure is driven mainly by renin and angiotensin, and others' mainly by salt and fluid volume [D4-01-F04]. A renin-angiotensin blocker works when the pressure is renin-driven; a diuretic works when it is volume-driven, which shows as low renin [D4-01-F06]. Calcium blockers act directly on the muscle of the arterioles and work across renin levels [D4-01-F06, D4-01-F13]. A salty diet suppresses renin, so a renin-angiotensin blocker then has less to block [D4-01-F13].

| Study | Who, where, how long | What it found |
|---|---|---|
| VA renin re-analysis [D4-01-F06] | 1,031 US men with renin measured, in a single-drug trial | At diastolic 95-99, hydrochlorothiazide worked in 82%, 78% and 14% of those with low, medium and high renin; captopril (an ACE inhibitor) in 51%, 83% and 100%; diltiazem (a calcium blocker) in 83%, 82% and 83%. Age and race predicted response better than renin (P<.001 against P=.05) |
| PEAR [D4-01-F14] | 363 US patients aged 65 or under (152 Black, 211 white), atenolol and hydrochlorothiazide in either order, home readings | Higher renin predicted more response to atenolol and less to hydrochlorothiazide, independent of race and age |
| Salt trial [D4-01-F13] | 391 salt-sensitive US patients, enalapril (an ACE inhibitor) against isradipine (a calcium blocker), alternating high salt (about 315 mmol sodium a day) and low salt (about 90) | The high-minus-low salt difference was -3.6/-1.6 to -8.1/-5.3 mmHg across groups with isradipine against -9.0/-5.3 to -11.8/-7.0 with enalapril: the calcium blocker lost less effect on high salt. On low salt the two drugs were similar |

#### Rotation and crossover trials

Chapter 2.3 gave PHYSIC's headline. In these trials each person takes several drug families in turn, so the trial can see whether a person's best drug differs from the average.

| Trial | Who, where, how long | What it found |
|---|---|---|
| PHYSIC [D4-01-F01, D4-01-F02, D4-01-F03] | Sweden, one centre, 280 randomised and 270 analysed (mean age 64, mild hypertension). Lisinopril 20 mg, candesartan 16 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg and amlodipine 10 mg in random order, two of them repeated; each period a 1-week placebo washout, 2 weeks of dose increase and at least 4 weeks at full dose; daytime ambulatory (24-hour monitor) readings | Each person's best drug gave 4.4 mmHg lower systolic pressure than a fixed choice, and 3.1 mmHg against lisinopril, the best on average; both are model estimates (claims check). Real differences between people appeared between a renin-angiotensin blocker and amlodipine or the thiazide. Large differences were excluded within those two pairs, which is not the same as none |
| Cambridge rotation [D4-01-F04] | 56 untreated young UK patients (mean 161/98), one month each on an ACE inhibitor (A), a beta-blocker (B), a calcium blocker (C) and a diuretic (D); 36 completed all four; 1999 | Control on one drug rose from 39% on the first drug to 73% on each person's best (p=0.0001). Responses to A and B went together (r=0.5), and to C and D (r=0.6), not across the pairs |
| GENRES [D4-01-F32] | 208 Finnish men aged 35-60; amlodipine 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg and losartan 50 mg for 4 weeks each, with 4-week placebo gaps; 24-hour readings | Median falls 11/8 (bisoprolol), 9/6 (losartan), 7/5 (amlodipine) and 5/2 mmHg (hydrochlorothiazide); the same AB/CD split. Amlodipine and thiazide responses grew with age, with higher pressure on placebo and with less night-time dipping. Men only |

PHYSIC's authors say the gain from choosing per person is about twice that of doubling a first drug's dose and more than half that of adding a second drug [D4-01-F03].

A warning comes from a larger data set. In individual data from 7 placebo-controlled trials of ACE-inhibitor regimens (28,281 people, change at 3 months, clinic readings), only 3% of the apparent spread in systolic response between people was real; the rest was ordinary variation [D4-03-F55]. OUR VIEW: the two findings fit. PHYSIC repeated each drug and used ambulatory readings, so it could see a real but modest difference between families; one patient's single before-and-after change mostly shows noise.

#### Traits that predict response

| Trait | What the trials show | India or South Asia |
|---|---|---|
| Age | Amlodipine's systolic effect is greater in older patients, "perhaps because of greater baseline systolic pressure" [D4-01-F18]. In an open US community trial of amlodipine (1,084 patients, 4 weeks of titration then 12 weeks, no placebo), 91.5% of those 65 or over reached goal against 84.1% under 65 [D4-01-F39]. The telmisartan label says its effect is "not influenced by patient age, gender, weight, or body mass index" [D4-01-F21] | No data found |
| Sex | In the same amlodipine trial 91.4% of women reached goal against 83.0% of men, not explained by weight, dose or compliance [D4-01-F39]. Ankle swelling on amlodipine, all doses pooled, was 14.6% in women against 5.6% in men [D4-01-F19]. Across 51 trials (358,636 people) each 5 mmHg fall cut heart events equally in women and men [D4-01-F38] | No data found |
| Salt | See the salt trial above [D4-01-F13] | North-east India, 374 volunteers, 7 days of low then 7 days of high salt: 47.6% of people with high pressure were salt-sensitive, and an extra-salt habit doubled the odds (OR 1.99) [D4-01-F47]. UK Bangladeshi patients with kidney disease (56, 6 months): low-salt advice lowered 24-hour pressure 8/2 mmHg on top of drugs [D4-01-F48] |
| African ancestry | 35 trials (25,540 people): calcium blockers and diuretics lowered pressure more than ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers [D4-01-F11]. CREOLE (728 Black patients, six sub-Saharan countries, 6 months): pairs containing amlodipine lowered 24-hour systolic pressure about 3 mmHg more than perindopril plus hydrochlorothiazide [D4-01-F12]. Telmisartan's effect is "noticeably less" in Black patients, "usually a low-renin population" [D4-01-F21] | Relevant to the Nigerian sheet |
| South Asian ancestry | ASCOT (UK and Nordic countries, 132 South Asian patients): adding perindopril (an ACE inhibitor) to amlodipine changed systolic pressure by -6.2 mmHg, against -1.7 in white and +0.8 in Black patients (interaction P=0.004) [D4-01-F07] | 16 trials with 1,719 South Asian patients, mostly in India, median 8 weeks, low quality: "no significant difference" between drug families [D4-01-F11] |
| Body weight | 232 obese patients, 12 weeks: lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide both worked [D4-01-F41]; no usable weight rule for the protocol drugs [D4-01-F42] | No data found |

#### What the guidelines do with this

- NICE (UK, 2019) is the only guideline found with an age and ancestry rule: an ACE inhibitor or ARB first for adults with type 2 diabetes, or under 55 and not of Black African or African-Caribbean origin; a calcium blocker first for those 55 or over, or of Black African or African-Caribbean origin, without diabetes [D4-01-F15]. It has no South Asian rule [D4-01-F15]. Its committee wrote: "No evidence for step 2 or step 3 treatment was identified that was relevant to determining the best sequence" [D4-01-F16].
- WHO 2021 lets any of three families start (thiazide-type, ACE inhibitor or ARB, long-acting calcium blocker), with no profile rule (search summary only) [D4-01-F43]. ISH 2020 has a rule for Black patients only (search summary only) [D4-01-F44]. ESH 2023 and the US 2017 guideline have no age-based first-drug rule [D4-01-F54].
- India's IHCI starts amlodipine 5 mg in every state except for chronic kidney disease, where telmisartan comes first, and budget-bound procurement was a stated reason [D4-01-F46]. The state documents say amlodipine needs no metabolic monitoring and can be given to women of childbearing age (search summary only) [D4-01-F46].

#### Gene tests and their limits

- In the Finnish GENRES study (228 men, each on four drugs), only one gene signal reached genome-wide significance, for bisoprolol, and it did not replicate [D4-01-F33]. Polygenic scores (built from 793 to over 1 million variants) did not predict response to any of the four drugs [D4-01-F34].
- The largest single-gene effect found was about 3 mmHg: the YEATS4 C/C genotype gave 3.4/2.5 mmHg more response to hydrochlorothiazide in 746 US patients, and it has not been tested in South Asians [D4-01-F35].
- A 2025 review says clinical use "remains challenging", polygenic scores for treatment remain "premature", each common variant moves systolic pressure by about 1 mmHg, and gene-based dosing advice exists for the beta-blocker metoprolol but not for amlodipine, telmisartan or the thiazides [D4-01-F36]. South Asian gene claims for amlodipine and ACE inhibitors are hypotheses in a teaching case, and ASCOT points the other way [D4-01-F37].

#### Raising a dose against adding a drug

| Analysis | Size | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Law and Wald 2003 [D4-01-F08] | 354 placebo-controlled trials, about 40,000 treated | Half the standard dose gave 20% less fall (7.1/4.4 against 9.1/5.5 mmHg); families added up; side effects of thiazides, beta-blockers and calcium blockers rose steeply with dose, while ARBs caused no excess symptoms |
| Wald 2009 [D4-01-F09] | 42 factorial trials, 10,968 people | Adding a second family roughly doubled the fall; doubling one drug's dose gave about one fifth (0.22) of that extra |
| Wang 2025 [D4-01-F10] | 484 placebo-controlled trials, 104,176 people, mean 8.6 weeks | A standard-dose single drug lowered systolic pressure 8.7 mmHg; each dose doubling added 1.5; a two-drug combination gave 14.9 |
| ARBs, Cochrane [D4-01-F52] | 46 trials, 13,451 people | Half the maximum dose gives 80% of the maximum fall; no ARB beat another |
| Thiazides, Cochrane [D4-01-F26] | 60 trials, 11,282 people, mean 8 weeks | Hydrochlorothiazide is dose-related (12.5 mg 6/3, 25 mg 8/3, 50 mg 11/5 mmHg); chlorthalidone 12.5-75 mg gave 12/4 mmHg with no dose dependence (low-quality evidence) |
| Quarter doses [D4-01-F27] | 42 trials, 20,284 people | Two drugs at a quarter dose each matched one drug at standard dose, with side effects no different from placebo |

The low-dose triple pill has been tested in South Asia. In TRIUMPH (Sri Lanka, 11 hospital clinics, 700 patients, 6 months, open-label, against usual care), one pill of telmisartan 20 mg, amlodipine 2.5 mg and chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (the protocol's three drugs at low dose) brought 70% to target against 55%, with dizziness, near-fainting or fainting in 5.2% against 2.8% [D4-01-F28]. GMRx2 (1,385 people in seven countries including Sri Lanka, double-blind, 12 weeks, funded by George Medicines) found a triple pill lowered home systolic pressure 2.5-5.4 mmHg more than each two-drug pair [D4-01-F29].

#### What each Gujarat step adds

The closest source is the US label of the telmisartan-amlodipine combination, whose trials use the Gujarat drugs and doses (8 weeks each; place not stated in the label).

| Gujarat step | Extra systolic fall | Cost of the step |
|---|---|---|
| 2. Amlodipine 5 to 10 mg | 5.3 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 18.2 - 12.9, placebo-subtracted, 1,461 patients) [D4-01-F49] | Ankle swelling 3.0% at 5 mg against 10.8% at 10 mg [D4-01-F19] |
| 3. Add telmisartan 40 mg | 4.0 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 22.2 - 18.2) [D4-01-F49]; 3.7 mmHg beyond staying on amlodipine 10 mg, in 947 patients not controlled on it [D4-01-F50] | Kidney and potassium checks (I6) |
| 4. Telmisartan 40 to 80 mg | 1.7 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 23.9 - 22.2) [D4-01-F49]; 0.2 mmHg in the 947 patients above (OUR ARITHMETIC: 11.3 - 11.1, a cross-arm difference not formally tested) [D4-01-F50]; -1 to +4 mmHg from the telmisartan label's ranges (OUR ARITHMETIC, as redone in the claims check) [D4-01-F21] | Four lab tests on the Gujarat sheet |
| 5. Add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg | About 6.2 mmHg when hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg was added to amlodipine 10 mg plus valsartan (another ARB), in 2,271 patients starting at 170/107, with no placebo arm [D4-01-F53] | Potassium, sodium, uric acid and sugar (I6) |

One more trial bears on step 2. In 1,097 patients not controlled on amlodipine 5 mg, adding telmisartan 40 mg lowered pressure 2.4/1.4 mmHg more than raising amlodipine to 10 mg, with ankle swelling in 4.3% against 27.2% [D4-01-F51]. And chlorthalidone 12.5 mg already sits near the top of its dose curve [D4-01-F26].

India's programme shows similar steps in practice. In Punjab, where step 2 raises amlodipine, clinic control among patients still in care went from 70% to 75%; in Maharashtra, where step 2 adds telmisartan 40 mg, from 76% to 81% [D4-01-F45]. These are control levels at the latest visit after a median 12 months of treatment, among patients who returned, not the effect of one 30-day step (claims check) [D4-02-F17].

**For the loop (OUR VIEW).** Adding or switching a drug family is where the millimetres are. Raising a dose buys little, and step 4 buys almost nothing while it triggers four lab tests. In South Asian patients no family stands out, so the protocol's fixed order is defensible, and age, sex and salt habit are the cheap traits worth recording. Gene and renin tests are not ready for the loop.

# D4-08 Claims check - biology part 3 (agent: claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-14)

## Summary

Checked 42 fact IDs from D4-02 "How fast a dose change works": every ID in its Digest and product section, plus the other time, interval and effect-size facts. Routes: openFDA label JSON (same set IDs as the note's DailyMed links), PubMed efetch, Europe PMC full-text XML, PMC HTML, guideline PDFs (WHO 2021, ISH 2020 author copy, IHCI Punjab and MP sheets, Swedish SmPC), the ESH 2023 and NICE pages. Verdicts: CONFIRMED 39, CORRECTED 1 (F34), CONTESTED 1 (F44), NOT FOUND 1 (F37). Every label number, steady-state time, guideline quote and trial number in the note matched its source.

Findings that change a step-timing rule:
1. F37 and the product section's 93 to 96% and 58 to 78%. Lasserson's model equation is behind a paywall, so the exponential shape is an unverified assumption. The arithmetic is right on that assumption. With a hyperbolic shape, or with the paper's own titration t50 of 1.2 weeks, the day 24 to 30 window holds about 79 to 92% of the full effect, and the day 8 to 14 window about 48 to 69%. Say "about 80 to 96%" and "about 48 to 78%". The 30-day default still looks sound; a 14-day step looks weaker than the note says.
2. F34 (Ojji 2024, Nigeria). The interval the note could not find is in the PMC full text: a first visit at 2 weeks, stepping up if clinic BP was 135/85 or more, justified by citing Lasserson ("almost all" of the effect by 2 weeks); the standard arm stepped monthly. The faster arm had more early eGFR falls of over 30% at month 1 (11% vs 4%, equal by month 6) and more potassium under 3.5 at month 6 (34% vs 18%). The arms also differed in drugs (indapamide). "No stops for adverse events" is true but incomplete. A fast ARB-plus-diuretic step would need an early creatinine and potassium check.
3. F44. The primary paper is still unopened (403, and a CAPTCHA that was not bypassed). Two news reports differ on the 12-week chlorthalidone ambulatory fall: 12.11 (Healio) against 11.1/7.8 (MDedge). Week 4 holds 56 to 61% of the 12-week effect on either figure, so "no fast track after chlorthalidone" is unchanged.

input.content:
### I4. How fast a dose change works

A step can only be judged once the new dose has had its full effect. Two clocks matter: the drug's blood level, which settles after 4 to 5 half-lives (the steady state), and the body's response, which can lag behind the blood level.

#### The two clocks, drug by drug

A drug reaches about 94-97% of its steady level after 4 to 5 half-lives (OUR ARITHMETIC, as in the note) [D4-02-F01].

| Drug | Half-life | Steady level reached | Time to (near) full effect | Label interval between dose steps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Amlodipine | 30-50 hours | 7-8 days [D4-02-F01] | Not stated in the label [D4-02-F03]; the effect builds slowly because binding is slow [D4-02-F02]; trough and peak effects are similar [D4-02-F04] | "In general, wait 7 to 14 days between titration steps" [D4-02-F03] |
| Telmisartan | About 24 hours | About 4-5 days (OUR ARITHMETIC: 24 hours x 4-5) [D4-02-F05] | US label: "Most of the antihypertensive effect is apparent within 2 weeks and maximal reduction is generally attained after 4 weeks" [D4-02-F06]. A European label: maximum "four to eight weeks after the start of treatment", to bear in mind "when considering raising the dose" [D4-02-F43] | Combination with hydrochlorothiazide: titrate "after 2 to 4 weeks" [D4-02-F07] |
| Losartan | 2 hours (active metabolite 6-9) | Not given | "substantially present within one week but in some studies the maximal effect occurred in 3-6 weeks" [D4-02-F13] | None given; one label trial stepped up "After one month" [D4-02-F13] |
| Chlorthalidone | About 40-60 hours | About 7-12 days (OUR ARITHMETIC: 40-60 hours x 4-5), from half-lives measured at 50-200 mg, not 12.5 mg (claims check) [D4-02-F08] | Office readings: most of the effect by week 2 [D4-02-F41]; 24-hour readings in a small Indian trial: still growing at 12 weeks [D4-02-F44] | 15 mg product: "After 2 weeks, the dosage may be increased" [D4-02-F09]; 12.5 mg product: may double after 2-4 weeks [D4-01-F23] |
| Hydrochlorothiazide | 5.6-14.8 hours | About 1-3 days (OUR ARITHMETIC: 5.6-14.8 hours x 5) [D4-02-F11] | With olmesartan, "near maximal at 4 weeks" [D4-02-F12] | None given [D4-02-F11] |

#### How much of the full effect arrives by when

A review of 18 trials (4,168 patients starting a first drug, office readings at least every 2 weeks for at least 4 weeks; abstract only) found that half of the maximum systolic fall arrived in 0.91 weeks, and adding the drug family did not improve the model, so the time course looked similar across families [D4-02-F36]. Where the trial raised the dose along the way, the half-time was longer (1.2 against 0.7 weeks) [D4-02-F36]. The claims check notes that none of these trials raised the dose of a drug already being taken, which is what the loop does; the 1.2-week figure is the closer match to a protocol step [D4-02-F36].

The share of the full effect reached by a given day depends on the shape of the curve, and the paper's equation could not be opened; it says only "asymptotic approach model" (the claims check could not find it) [D4-02-F37]. ASSUMPTION of an exponential curve: about 53% at 1 week, 78% at 2 weeks and 95% at 4 weeks (OUR ARITHMETIC: 1 - 0.5^(weeks / 0.91)) [D4-02-F37]. With a hyperbolic curve instead, about 69% at 2 weeks and 82% at 4 (OUR ARITHMETIC, by the claims check) [D4-02-F37]. ESH 2023 says that with two-drug combinations the fall is expected "within 1-2 weeks", with a smaller further decline for a few more weeks, and that a single drug is slower [D4-02-F20].

The thiazides need a closer look. In the Thalitone trials (222 patients, 12 weeks, placebo-controlled), the average office fall over weeks 4-12 (-12.43 mmHg) was only slightly larger than over weeks 2-12 (-11.77) [D4-02-F10]; that product is a 15 mg formulation with enhanced absorption, not generic 12.5 mg chlorthalidone (claims check) [D4-04-F15]. In a US crossover trial in untreated patients (30 completed the first period, office readings every 2 weeks), chlorthalidone 12.5 mg lowered office systolic pressure 15.7 mmHg by week 2 [D4-02-F41]. But in an Indian double-blind trial (54 patients with mild hypertension, 12 weeks; abstract only; the first author and two co-authors are from the drug maker Ipca Laboratories), chlorthalidone 6.25 mg lowered ambulatory systolic pressure 6.74 mmHg at 4 weeks [D4-02-F44]. Two news reports disagree on the 12-week fall: 12.11 mmHg in one, 11.1/7.8 mmHg in another; on either figure about 56-61% of the 12-week effect was present at week 4 (OUR ARITHMETIC: 6.74 / 12.11 and 6.74 / 11.1; contested in the claims check) [D4-02-F44]. In the same trial hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg lowered office pressure but not 24-hour pressure, because it wears off within the day; the authors say it "merely converted sustained hypertension into masked hypertension" [D4-02-F42].

#### What the guidelines say about the interval

| Source | Interval between steps |
|---|---|
| Punjab IHCI sheet | "After 30 days" at each step, with a footnote: "Dose of anti-hypertension medications can be titrated at 15 days frequency if required" [D4-02-F15] |
| Madhya Pradesh IHCI sheet | 30 days at each step; no faster option [D4-02-F16] |
| Nigeria sheet | 1 month [D4-02-F33] |
| WHO 2021 | Monthly until target (conditional, low-certainty evidence), then every 3-6 months. The rationale says the intervals "should be viewed as suggestions and may be modified", and cites a UK cohort of 88,756 adults in which re-evaluation later than 2.7 months after starting gave a hazard ratio of 1.18 for major heart events (claims check) [D4-02-F18] |
| ISH 2020 | "Aim for BP control within 3 months"; no step interval [D4-02-F19] |
| ESH 2023 | Starting treatment "may be evaluated monthly", but "three large observational studies and one small RCT suggest" 2-weekly visits bring earlier control; visit frequency "should not be subjected to rigid rules" [D4-02-F20]. Avoid "a long titration period" with uncontrolled pressure; doctors not stepping up is a major cause of poor control [D4-02-F21] |
| NICE NG136 | No interval; check doses and adherence before the next step [D4-02-F22] |
| US guidance | Monthly until controlled (search summary only; wording not verified) [D4-02-F23] |

#### Trials that stepped faster

| Study | Design | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Godwin 2010, Canada [D4-02-F24] | Cluster trial, 19 family doctors, 156 patients: a visit every 2 weeks for 16 weeks with the regimen adjusted, against usual care; abstract only | At 12 months office systolic pressure fell 14.7 against 2.7 mmHg; side effects not in the abstract; only 74% and 71% analysed |
| Turchin 2010, US [D4-02-F25] | Cohort, 5,042 patients with diabetes | Visits every 2 weeks or less brought pressure to normal in a median 0.7 months against 1.9; observational |
| Sherman 2018, US [D4-02-F26] | Cohort, 95,957 newly diagnosed patients | The longer the gap between visits, the less control; observational |
| TASMINH4, UK [D4-02-F28] | Trial, 1,182 patients; home readings each month for GPs to use in titration, against usual care | "Adverse events were similar between all three groups" |
| Ishak 2024, US [D4-02-F31] | Pilot, 42 patients, pharmacist telehealth with expedited titration, no control group | "no instances of falls or hypotension" |
| Ojji 2024, Nigeria [D4-02-F34] | Open-label trial, 300 Black African adults, 6 months: a low-dose triple pill (telmisartan, amlodipine, indapamide) with a first visit at 2 weeks and a step up at clinic 135/85 or more, against the Nigeria protocol stepped monthly at 140/90 or more (interval corrected in the claims check) | Home systolic pressure fell 31 against 26 mmHg; home control 62% against 28%; no one stopped for adverse events. But the faster arm had more eGFR falls of over 30% at month 1 (11% against 4%, equal at 9% by month 6) and more potassium under 3.5 at month 6 (34% against 18%). The arms used different drugs, so the trial does not isolate the effect of stepping faster (claims check) |
| Asian amlodipine pool [D4-02-F32] | Maker-run trials, 174 Asian patients (none from India), 4-8 weeks on 5 mg then 4-8 weeks on 10 mg; no placebo | A further 13.3/9.2 mmHg fall, inflated by regression to the mean; ankle swelling 6.3% |
| Scotland 1987 [D4-02-F35] | 30 patients, amlodipine 2.5 to 10 mg "titrated at 2 weekly intervals" over 8 weeks, against placebo | Well tolerated; 2 patients had slight ankle swelling on 10 mg |

Once pressure is controlled, 6-monthly review was as good as 3-monthly in a 3-year trial of 609 patients in Ontario [D4-02-F27]. No trial was found that randomised 2-week against 4-week steps and counted side effects.

#### The 30-day step, drug by drug

OUR ARITHMETIC from the 18-trial model, with the curve shape an ASSUMPTION [D4-02-F36, D4-02-F37]: readings on days 24-30 see about 80-96% of the full effect (exponential with a half-time of 0.91 weeks gives 93-96%, the titration half-time of 1.2 weeks gives 86-92%, a hyperbolic curve gives 79-83%). A 14-day step read on days 8-14 would see only about 48-78%.

| Step | Steady level by day 24 | Verdict on the 30-day step and the day 24-30 window (OUR VIEW) |
|---|---|---|
| 2. Amlodipine 10 mg | Yes (7-8 days) [D4-02-F01] | 30 days is sound. A 15-day step has support for this step alone in the label, the Punjab sheet and the 1987 trial [D4-02-F03, D4-02-F15, D4-02-F35]: a clinician's option, not tonight's |
| 3. Add telmisartan 40 mg | Yes (4-5 days) [D4-02-F05] | Fits the US label's maximum at about 4 weeks; keep 30 days. Ojji's faster ARB-plus-diuretic arm had more early kidney-function falls [D4-02-F34] |
| 4. Telmisartan 80 mg | Yes [D4-02-F05] | Keep 30 days; the European label's 4-8 weeks argues against stepping faster [D4-02-F43] |
| 5. Add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg | Yes (7-12 days) [D4-02-F08] | Keep 30 days; the 24-hour effect may still be growing [D4-02-F44], so a mean just above the line may deserve one more cycle at the same dose |
| 5 with hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg | Yes (1-3 days) [D4-02-F11] | Keep 30 days; because it is short-acting, a morning reading before the tablet catches its lowest level, so record the dose time [D4-02-F42] |

**For the loop (OUR VIEW).** The 30-day step and the day 24-30 window fit the biology: every protocol drug is at its steady level by day 24, and most of the effect is in on any curve shape. Faster steps have mostly observational support and thin side-effect data, the one trial with side-effect numbers saw early kidney and potassium changes, and India's programme did not record side effects [D4-02-F34, D4-02-F17]. A 15-day option for amlodipine is a later choice for a clinician.

### I5. Natural variation and how many readings

Blood pressure moves on its own, from minute to minute, morning to evening, day to day and season to season, while a protocol step changes it by only 2 to 6 mmHg (I3). This section measures the movement and works out how many readings it takes to see a step.

#### Why the number moves

- **The alerting reaction.** In 48 people with a pressure line in the artery (Italy, 1983), a doctor's arrival and cuff measurement raised pressure within 1-4 minutes by a mean 26.7/14.9 mmHg (range 4-75 systolic), with heart rate up 15.9 beats a minute; it settled over a 10-15 minute visit and came back at a second visit [D4-03-F53]. In 65 people in Germany, an arrival reading was raised, and 10-18 minutes of rest lowered pressure by about 10 mmHg [D4-03-F54].
- **Getting used to measuring.** Home readings fall over the first days and level off after day 3; day 1 runs about 2.8/1.4 mmHg high (2,122 people, Finland, Greece, UK) [D4-03-F01]. In treated UK patients day 1 was 3.5 mmHg above day 7 in the first months, and the gap faded after 6 months of self-monitoring [D4-03-F16].
- **Two readings in a sitting.** The second reading averaged 2.3 mmHg lower than the first but was higher in 31.7% of pairs (175 Japanese kidney patients) [D4-03-F36]; first, second and averaged morning readings predicted heart events equally well (Japan, treated patients) [D4-03-F37].
- **The day's rhythm.** A normal "dipper" falls 10-20% at night; less than 10% is non-dipping [D4-03-F50]. In India, 11.9% of 27,472 primary-care patients had high pressure only at night [D4-03-F39]. In 519 older Japanese patients, the top tenth of morning surge (55 mmHg or more) had more strokes (19% against 7.3%) [D4-03-F46], but a review of 17 studies found no agreed surge threshold [D4-03-F47]. Evening home readings ran 3.8 mmHg above morning ones in untreated and 0.9 mmHg in treated Finnish adults (OUR ARITHMETIC: 141.5 - 137.7; 137.1 - 136.2; 1,919 people) [D4-03-F23]; in treated patients in Argentina the average gap was 1.1 mmHg, with a spread (SD) of 12.5 mmHg between people [D4-03-F24].
- **Seasons.** Japanese home readings peak in December-January and are lowest in July-August, about 3-4 mmHg apart (7,908 people) [D4-03-F28]. Indian figures are larger but are not home-cuff readings. In Punjab, 978 people from a general community sample were measured in all four seasons by trained nurses at home or work: winter ran 9.01/5.61 mmHg above summer, and 10 degrees C colder went with 3.9/2.1 mmHg higher pressure; the cited mechanism is that cold raises sympathetic drive and tightens vessels [D4-03-F31]. In 132 young women with normal pressure in a Delhi slum, measured at investigator home visits, winter ran 11.07/6.79 mmHg higher [D4-03-F32]. ESH says home monitoring can help adjust treatment in people with large seasonal swings [D4-03-F30].
- **Regression to the mean.** People chosen because a reading was high are partly chosen for a random high error that does not repeat. In 286 Australians measured every 3 months, those starting at a home systolic mean of 156 fell to 143 within a year, and those at 113 rose to 120, in both trial arms [D4-03-F26]. In the UK HOME BP trial the usual-care group fell 9.8 mmHg in a year (OUR ARITHMETIC: 151.6 - 141.8) [D4-03-F57].

#### How big the movement is

| Level | Spread (systolic) | Who | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| One reading within a week | SD 11.8 mmHg, 11.0 after 6 months | 225 treated UK patients, mean age about 67 | [D4-03-F10] |
| One reading, 95% band around the weekly mean | About plus or minus 23 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 1.96 x 11.8) | Same | [D4-03-F62] |
| Difference between two weekly means | SD 10.11 (1 day), 6.37 (3 days), 4.36 mmHg (7 days) | 316 untreated US adults, mean home pressure 115/77 | [D4-03-F33] |
| Error band of a 3-day mean | About plus or minus 8.8 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 6.37 / 1.414 x 1.96) | Same | [D4-03-F34] |
| Error band of a 7-day mean | About plus or minus 6.0 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 4.36 / 1.414 x 1.96) | Same | [D4-03-F34] |
| 3-day mean against 7-day mean | Off by 3.66 mmHg on average at month 1, 2.91 at month 6 | 84 treated UK patients | [D4-03-F06] |
| A week's or a month's set of readings, around each person's own trend | SD 4.7 and 5.1 mmHg (the model's leftover scatter, as the claims check words it) | 232 and 582 treated UK patients on unchanged drugs | [D4-03-F11] |
| Weekday against weekend | 0.5-1.8 mmHg | 754 Finnish workers | [D4-03-F35] |

The claims check adds a caution: the 3-day and 7-day figures come from untreated young adults, and treated older patients vary more (11.8 mmHg above), so the real bands for the loop's patients are probably wider [D4-03-F34, D4-03-F10].

#### How many readings are enough

- A review of 37 studies: 3 days gave 72-91% of the best possible prediction of outcomes and 7 days 86-96%; the authors advise 3 days, extended to 7 only when the mean is near a threshold [D4-03-F02].
- In 316 untreated US adults, 3 days of morning and evening readings were needed for a reliable mean [D4-03-F03]; in 361, with an upper and a lower cut-off, 63.7% could be classed after 1 day and almost all within 3 [D4-03-F04].
- ESH 2021: 7 days, "not fewer than 3"; whether to discard day 1 is "matter of debate" [D4-03-F07], and sources disagree [D4-03-F17].
- An Asian expert schedule, "722": 2 readings, twice a day, for 7 days [D4-03-F09].

#### White-coat and masked high pressure in India

White-coat means high in clinic but normal at home; masked means normal in clinic but high at home (home line 135/85, clinic line 140/90) [D4-03-F42].

| Study | Who | White-coat | Masked |
|---|---|---|---|
| India Heart Study [D4-03-F21] | 18,918 untreated people, 1,237 primary-care doctors across India, 1 week of home readings | 23.7% | 18.2% |
| India ambulatory study [D4-03-F39] | 27,472 primary-care patients, 45.5% treated, 24-hour readings | 12.0% | 19.3% (23.0% untreated, 14.8% treated) |
| GRAND [D4-03-F40] | 1,578 treated patients analysed of 1,920 enrolled, 18 centres, 12 states | 5.1% (white-coat uncontrolled) | 21.8% (masked uncontrolled) |

These labels are not stable. In a meta-analysis of 15 studies (5,729 people), a masked label from home readings agreed with a repeat at kappa 0.26 (kappa measures agreement beyond chance; 1 is perfect), and a white-coat label at 0.18, "slight agreement" [D4-03-F44]. In North India only 18.1% of 2,588 people with high pressure or their carers used home monitoring, and observed technique was excellent in 15.9% of patients [D4-03-F58].

#### How big a change must be to be real

| Comparison | Smallest change beyond noise (95%) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Two 3-day means a week apart | 12.5 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 1.96 x 6.37) | [D4-03-F34] |
| Two 7-day means a week apart | 8.5 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 1.96 x 4.36) | [D4-03-F34] |
| Two months on unchanged drugs | 13.0-14.1 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 4.7-5.1 x 1.414 x 1.96) | [D4-03-F61] |

All three come from data that probably understate the spread in treated older patients (claims check) [D4-03-F34]. Two studies show what happens when noise is read as change. On fixed drugs, a patient starting at a home mean of 130 had an 18% chance of reading 135 or more at a 6-month retest, and only a 25% chance that such a rise was real [D4-03-F11]. In clinic data from 1,709 patients on fixed drugs (the PROGRESS trial), a rise of more than 10 mmHg gave 6 false alarms for every true rise [D4-03-F15].

#### What self-titration trials required before a step

| Trial | Readings | Rule before changing a drug |
|---|---|---|
| TASMIN-SR, UK [D4-03-F13] | First week of each month, mornings, two readings 5 minutes apart; the second one used | "Four or more above target readings in two consecutive weeks"; each step of the plan after "two consecutive months of raised readings" |
| TASMINH4, UK [D4-03-F18] | Twice morning and evening, first week of every month | A web page averaged each week; clinicians reviewed monthly; home targets under 135/85 (under 80 years), 145/85 (80 or over), 135/75 (diabetes) |
| HOME BP, UK, 622 patients [D4-03-F56] | Two morning readings for 7 days each month, the second entered, after a 7-day practice week | A change only "When mean home blood pressure was above target for two consecutive months"; clinic systolic 3.4 mmHg lower than usual care at a year |
| HOMEBP schedule rule [D4-03-F14] | 7 days | After 3 controlled months, measure every 8 weeks; back to monthly at 135/85 or more |
| Australia, 286 patients [D4-03-F38] | 7 days | 3 or more of the last 10 readings at 135 or more best predicted uncontrolled 24-hour pressure (area under the curve 0.71, where 0.5 is chance) |

Earlier trials that used the clinic target of 140/90 for home readings controlled pressure worse [D4-03-F19], and ESH 2021 says dose self-adjustment is "to be avoided, if not under guidance by the physician in charge" [D4-03-F07]. No published home-titration trial was found that used a formal statistical rule; all used simple counting rules like these.

**For the loop (OUR VIEW).** A step's 2-6 mmHg is smaller than the noise between two monthly means, so the loop should judge where the mean sits against the line, not how far it moved since the last cycle. A 7-day block narrows the error band from about 9 to about 6 mmHg, and the wider spread in treated older patients argues for 7 days whenever the mean is near the line. The UK trials waited for two months above target before a change.

### I6. Why each safety check exists

Each safety rule exists because of a specific piece of physiology. This section gives the mechanism, the numbers and the time window for each.

#### The kidney after telmisartan

**Mechanism.** Angiotensin II keeps the efferent arteriole tight, which holds up the pressure that drives filtration [D4-04-F52]. Blocking it "causes selectively greater vasodilatation of the efferent arterioles of the glomeruli, resulting in a decline of the intraglomerular filtration pressure", so GFR falls and creatinine (a waste product the kidney clears, measured in blood) rises [D4-04-F26]. KDIGO treats a small early rise as expected [D4-05-F28]. Two situations make the fall bigger. When both kidney arteries are narrowed, filtration depends on that angiotensin II tone, and ACE inhibitors are "contraindicated in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis due to risk of azotemia" (a rise in blood urea and creatinine); the ARB labels "anticipate an effect similar" [D4-04-F52, D4-04-F04]. And when a patient is short of salt and water, for example on high-dose diuretics, pressure leans more on angiotensin II, so blocking it drops pressure more [D4-04-F09].

**How much rise, and what to do.**

| Source | Applies to | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Telmisartan label | All patients | Creatinine rise of 0.5 mg/dL or more in 0.4% on telmisartan against 0.3% on placebo; no numeric threshold or recheck interval [D4-04-F05, D4-04-F04] |
| Bakris and Weir 2000 | 12 trials of ACE inhibitors, 1,102 people with reduced kidney function, about 3 years | Rises "of up to 30% that stabilize within the first 2 months" went with long-term kidney protection; withdrawal only if the rise exceeds 30% within 2 months or potassium is 5.6 mmol/l or more (claims check) [D4-04-F21] |
| UK Kidney Association 2026 | Every ACE inhibitor or ARB start | Urea and electrolytes before; recheck "at 1-2 weeks after initiation of ACE-I or ARB and after every dose titration" (grade 1A, the strongest grade) [D4-04-F34] |
| NICE NG203 | Adults with chronic kidney disease | Potassium and eGFR before, and 1-2 weeks after starting and after each dose rise. Under a 25% eGFR fall or 30% creatinine rise: no change, repeat in 1-2 weeks. At 25% or 30% or more: look for other causes (dehydration, NSAID painkillers), then stop or cut the dose [D4-04-F23] |
| KDIGO 2021 and 2024 | Adults with chronic kidney disease | Check pressure, creatinine and potassium within 2-4 weeks of starting or raising the dose, "depending on the current GFR and serum potassium"; the rise "will typically happen during the first 2 weeks" and "should stabilize within 2-4 weeks"; continue "unless serum creatinine rises by more than 30% within 4 weeks"; no trial has tested any cut-off [D4-04-F27, D4-05-F27, D4-05-F28] |
| IHCI Telangana and Maharashtra sheets | India | Baseline labs only; no recheck after telmisartan starts. Both sheets prefer an ACE inhibitor or ARB in kidney disease if "close clinical and biochemical monitoring" is possible, with no test or interval named (claims check) [D4-04-F57] |

The claims check notes that a 30% creatinine rise is about a 25% eGFR fall, so the two cut-offs are not the same size [D4-05-F28]. Rises below 30% are not fully harmless. In 122,363 UK people starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB (1997-2014, observational), death rates were 1.15 times higher after a 10-19% rise and 1.35 times after a 20-29% rise, against under 10%; 1.7% had rises of 30% or more, with end-stage kidney disease 3.43 times and death 1.84 times as frequent [D4-04-F22]. The rise may mark a sicker patient rather than cause the harm [D4-04-F22]. In ONTARGET (25,620 high-risk patients, median 56 months), telmisartan 80 mg and ramipril 10 mg gave the same main outcome, while combining an ARB with an ACE inhibitor raised kidney dysfunction (13.5% against 10.2%) with no extra benefit, which is the basis of "never combine" rules [D4-04-F55].

#### Potassium

**Mechanism.** Potassium sets the resting electrical charge of heart muscle cells, and the most serious results of high potassium are "arrhythmias and cardiac arrest"; small further rises can move fast "from peaked T waves to ventricular fibrillation or asystole" [D4-04-F35]. The ECG may be normal even when potassium is very high, so only a blood test can rule it out [D4-04-F35]. An ARB pushes potassium up because blocking angiotensin II blunts aldosterone [D4-04-F26]. A thiazide pushes it down: blocking the salt transporter in the distal tubule sends more sodium to the collecting duct, where it is swapped for potassium (textbook physiology, not stated in the label) [D4-05-F21]. Both directions matter. In 911,698 US patient records, death was least common at 4.0 to under 5.0 mEq/L and rose with every 0.1 step below 4.0 or from 5.0 up (observational) [D4-04-F36]. In a US case-control study (114 sudden cardiac arrests, 535 controls), thiazide dose went with arrest: 100 mg had odds of 3.6 against 25 mg, and adding a potassium-sparing drug cut the odds (0.3) [D4-04-F37].

**Thresholds.**

| Potassium (mmol/l) | Action |
|---|---|
| Above 5.0 before starting | Caution (UKKA); NICE, for kidney disease: do not routinely start [D4-04-F34, D4-04-F24] |
| 5.5-5.9 (mild) | Repeat "within 3 days, or as soon as feasible" if found unexpectedly in the community; monitor more often and consider a lower dose [D4-04-F34] |
| 6.0-6.4 (moderate) | Repeat within 1 day; stop the ACE inhibitor or ARB in patients who do not qualify for potassium-binding drugs (UKKA wording, claims check) [D4-04-F34]; NICE: stop at 6.0 or more once other potassium-raising drugs are stopped [D4-04-F24] |
| 6.5 or more (severe) | Admit at once [D4-04-F34] |

KDIGO adds that high potassium on an ARB can often be managed (diet, drug review, binders) rather than by stopping, because stopping is linked to more heart events [D4-05-F31]. On telmisartan alone, multiple-dose studies found "no clinically significant changes" in potassium [D4-04-F06]; the risk comes with kidney disease, heart failure, potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics and "potassium-containing salt substitutes" [D4-04-F06, D4-04-F07]. NICE says potassium-chloride salt substitutes should not be used by older people, people with diabetes or kidney disease, or people taking ACE inhibitors or ARBs [D4-04-F28]. On the thiazide side, chlorthalidone caused more low potassium than hydrochlorothiazide in the Diuretic Comparison Project (13,523 US veterans aged 65 or over, 2.4 years: 6.0% against 4.4%), with no difference in heart outcomes [D4-04-F33]. Low magnesium makes low potassium "difficult to treat despite potassium repletion" [D4-04-F15].

#### Pregnancy

**Mechanism.** In the second and third trimesters, drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system reduce the fetus's kidney function [D4-04-F02]. The fetus makes less urine, so the amniotic fluid drains (oligohydramnios); the lungs cannot grow (lung hypoplasia) and the squeezed fetus gets skull and limb deformities; newborns can have no urine, low pressure, kidney failure, or die [D4-04-F02]. Timing matters because amniotic fluid grows from 10-20 ml at 10 weeks to about 800 ml at 24 weeks, and in late pregnancy fetal urine is one of its two main sources [D4-04-F56]. In 14 fetuses or newborns who died after second- or third-trimester exposure, autopsy found malformed kidney tubules, and the lesions may persist after the drug is stopped [D4-04-F54]. In published case reports, 13% of ARB-exposed newborns had no complications against 52% after ACE inhibitors (72 reports, biased toward bad outcomes) [D4-04-F53].

**First trimester.** In Tennessee (29,507 infants), first-trimester-only ACE-inhibitor exposure went with any major malformation at a risk ratio of 2.71 against no blood-pressure drug [D4-04-F31]. In California (465,754 mother-infant pairs), heart defects after first-trimester ACE inhibitors had an odds ratio of 1.14 against mothers with untreated high pressure [D4-04-F32]. These measure different outcomes; the like-for-like figure from the California study, any birth defect against hypertensive mothers, was an adjusted odds ratio of 0.97 (claims check) [D4-04-F32]. Both are ACE-inhibitor data, not ARB data [D4-04-F31, D4-04-F32]. OUR VIEW: the clear danger window for the protocol's ARB is the second and third trimesters, and first-trimester exposure is a reason to switch quickly.

**The labels and the rule.** A generic telmisartan label made in India (revised March 2025; maker corrected in the claims check) carries a boxed warning: "When pregnancy is detected, discontinue telmisartan as soon as possible" [D4-04-F01]; losartan's label says the same [D4-04-F03]. Thiazides cross the placenta and "can cause placental hypoperfusion"; chlorthalidone "should not be used as first-line therapy to treat hypertension in pregnancy" but carries no boxed warning [D4-04-F17]. Amlodipine's label says the data "are not sufficient to inform a drug-associated risk" [D4-04-F14], and the IHCI sheets allow calcium blockers [D4-04-F57]. NICE NG133 says to stop an ACE inhibitor or ARB "preferably within 2 working days of notification of pregnancy" and offer alternatives: labetalol first, nifedipine if labetalol is unsuitable, methyldopa if both are unsuitable [D4-04-F29, D4-04-F30].

#### Dizziness on standing in older people

**Mechanism.** Standing pools 25-30% of the blood in the legs and the gut circulation, so less returns to the heart and pressure falls [D4-04-F47]. Pressure sensors in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch (the baroreflex) detect the fall and signal the brainstem, which raises heart rate and tightens arterioles and veins [D4-04-F46]. With age the baroreflex, fluid volume and vein tone all weaken, and blood-pressure drugs and diuretics add to it; after a meal the gut's blood volume rises 200-300%, so pressure can drop after eating [D4-04-F46]. Orthostatic hypotension is a fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 diastolic after at least 1 minute standing, measured from lying (or seated if lying is impractical, repeating from lying if a seated test is negative despite symptoms) [D4-04-F38].

| Finding | Source |
|---|---|
| 22.2% of community adults over 60 (20 studies, 24,967 people) | [D4-04-F39] |
| Kerala, 240 older people: 9.6%; a drop in the first minute went with falls (odds 1.97); each extra medicine raised the odds of orthostatic hypotension 1.73 | [D4-04-F40] |
| A first-minute drop was found in 29.0% by continuous measurement but in 5.6% by an ordinary cuff (13 studies, 5,465 people 65 or over) | [D4-04-F41] |
| Falls: odds 1.73 (50 studies, 49,164 people, unadjusted) | [D4-04-F42] |
| Hip fracture 43% more common in the first 45 days after starting any blood-pressure drug (Ontario, 301,591 people, self-controlled case series) | [D4-04-F48] |
| ALLHAT (23,964 people 65 or over, 4.9 years, randomised): no long-term difference between drugs, but more falls on amlodipine in the first year against chlorthalidone (HR 2.24), which the authors say needs confirmation | [D4-04-F49] |
| Lower pressure goals did not raise orthostatic hypotension in 5 open-label trials (18,466 people; odds 0.93), though the trials measured from seated and missed first-minute drops | [D4-04-F44] |

**Testing at home.** In 25 older patients in north-east England, a patient-led lying-to-standing test at home agreed with the clinician's in 95% (kappa 0.90), though single readings differed by up to 17-20 mmHg [D4-04-F50]. In 4,556 Swedish adults, two home standing readings found a drop in 6.4% [D4-04-F51].

#### Sodium, uric acid and sugar on thiazides

- **Sodium.** Thiazides block the sodium-chloride transporter in the distal convoluted tubule, the segment that dilutes urine, so the kidney cannot pass free water well; drinking a lot and eating little (low solute intake) make it worse [D4-04-F60]. In Denmark (2014-2018, age 40 or over), 3.83% of new bendroflumethiazide users and 3.51% of new users of a hydrochlorothiazide combination pill had sodium under 130 mmol/l within 2 years; hazard ratios were 3.56 and 4.25 in the first 30 days and 1.26 and 1.29 after a year, while the labels call it rare [D4-04-F58]. Risk rises with age and low body weight: in Hong Kong (223 cases, 216 controls), each 10 years of age gave a hazard ratio of 2.14 and each 5 kg more weight cut the odds (0.77) [D4-04-F61]. In Taiwan, older patients with thiazide-linked low sodium died more often (HR 1.39) [D4-04-F59]. The one Indian study (Lucknow) found low sodium in 27% of outpatients on diuretics for 6 months or more, and new cases in 18% at 3 months and 29% at 6 months; of 247 hospitalised low-sodium cases of any cause (mean age about 50), 45% were admitted in April-June and 46.6% in October-March, diuretic use was not significant in the multivariate analysis, and thiazides were the commonest class (corrected in the claims check) [D4-04-F62]. Season is therefore at most a soft flag.
- **Uric acid.** Thiazides cut the kidney's clearance of uric acid and "may precipitate gout in susceptible patients" [D4-04-F16]. In 5,789 US adults followed for 9 years, thiazides raised gout risk (HR 1.44), and the link vanished after adjusting for uric acid, so it runs through uric acid; starting a diuretic raised uric acid 0.72 mg/dL more [D4-04-F63].
- **Sugar.** Thiazide labels report dose-related rises in blood glucose and say "latent diabetes mellitus may become manifest" [D4-04-F15, D4-04-F19]. Across 59 trials, the more potassium fell, the more glucose rose (r = -0.54); the proposed reason is that low potassium reduces insulin release [D4-04-F64].

#### Ankle swelling on amlodipine

Widening the arterioles is thought to raise pressure inside the capillaries, so fluid leaks into the ankles [D4-04-F65]. Swelling is dose-related: 1.8% at 2.5 mg, 3.0% at 5 mg and 10.8% at 10 mg, against 0.6% on placebo [D4-04-F11]. Across all doses it was 14.6% in women and 5.6% in men [D4-04-F12]. In 106 trials (99,469 patients), calcium blockers caused swelling in 10.7% against 3.2%, rising to 24% after 6 months, and in 16.1% at high dose against 5.7% at low dose [D4-04-F65]. Adding an ARB or ACE inhibitor cut it by 38% [D4-04-F66]. It is common in Indian practice: 23.9% of 800 amlodipine patients in a Mumbai hospital record study had swelling at some point [D4-04-F67], and an unpublished IHCI survey found about 12% on amlodipine 10 mg [D4-02-F17].

#### What 180/110 means

Pressure this high without symptoms is called urgency; an emergency is very high pressure "associated with acute organ damage" in the heart, eyes, brain, kidneys or large arteries [D4-04-F70]. Among 59,836 Cleveland Clinic office visits at 180/110 or more (2008-2013), matched patients sent home (852) and sent to hospital (426) had major heart events at 7 days in 0 and 0.5%; patients referred for symptoms were excluded, and hospital referral brought more admissions without better outcomes [D4-04-F68]. In Italy, such a reading marked a worse risk profile and a five-fold higher chance of staying uncontrolled [D4-04-F69]. Long-standing high pressure "shifts the lower and upper blood pressure limits of CBF autoregulation towards higher pressure" (the brain's self-protection of its blood flow), and a fall cuts brain blood flow only once pressure drops below the lower limit; with treatment the limits may re-adapt [D4-04-F72]. OUR VIEW: a fast fall in such a person is more likely to cross the raised lower limit, which argues against bringing pressure down fast at home. A gradual lowering in 37 people over 70 (reviews every 2 weeks, 12 weeks, intensive against usual target) raised brain blood flow [D4-04-F73]. NICE sends a person at 180/120 to same-day care only with eye signs or "life-threatening symptoms such as new onset confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure, or acute kidney injury" [D4-04-F71]. The sheets differ: Telangana refers "after starting treatment", Maharashtra starts treatment and refers immediately [D4-04-F57], and Nigeria gives step 3 drugs and sends the patient to emergency within 1 hour [D4-02-F33].

**For the loop (OUR VIEW).** Each check matches a mechanism and a window. Kidney and potassium tests belong in the 1-4 weeks after telmisartan starts or rises; sodium and potassium tests in the first month of a thiazide, first for older and thinner patients; a pregnancy question at every cycle while a barred drug is taken; a standing check in older patients in the weeks after each step; and a symptom question, not a faster dose, at a very high reading.
